docs.title: Spark on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Submit and observe Spark applications from Python, the CLI or Airflow using your existing Kubernetes cluster. Optional API and shared web-console components make applications, logs and diagnostics accessible to operators. Spark creates the executors; your cluster and applications retain their infrastructure and data responsibilities.

What's new

The release notes list every published release and the release in preparation, whichever documentation version you are reading.

Start here Install

You can use the core Python client or CLI without deploying the API or Airflow. Spark and Java run in the application image; they are not required on the submitting machine. See Spark compatibility for image requirements.

docs.title: Choose what to run
docs.text:
• Submit an application

    Run an existing Python or JVM application from the Python client or the CLI, then wait for it, stream its logs or cancel it.

    Your first Kubernetes job

  • Portable job files and SQL

    Describe jobs in versioned files with profiles, preview them offline, and run SQL files or inline statements.

    Job files · SQL jobs

  • Spark Connect and notebooks

    Use an existing Spark Connect endpoint, or create a private server for a notebook or interactive session.

    Spark Connect · Jupyter

  • Schedule with Airflow

    Run Spark applications and SQL from Airflow 2.11 or 3, with deferrable waiting and a native Airflow 3 task tab.

    Airflow

  • Observe and diagnose

    List applications, read logs and open the Spark UI from the web console, and explain Pending or failed drivers.

    Diagnostics · Run history

  • Deploy the API

    Install the API, console and optional History Server with the Helm chart, and accept approved remote submissions.

    Chart deployment · Remote submission

Try the ETL starter locally before configuring a cluster, or run dbt with temporary Spark compute through the experimental dbt adapter.

docs.title: How the pieces fit
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph clients [Where you submit]
    sdk[Python client]
    cli[CLI]
    airflow[Airflow operators]
    remote[Remote CLI]
  end
  api[API and web console]
  subgraph cluster [Your Kubernetes namespace]
    driver[Spark driver pod]
    executors[Executor pods]
    history[Spark History Server]
  end
  sdk & cli & airflow --> k8s[(Kubernetes API)]
  remote -- approved jobs --> api
  api --> k8s
  k8s --> driver
  driver -- creates --> executors
  api -. logs, Spark UI proxy .-> driver
  api -. proxy .-> history

Every route creates the driver pod through the Kubernetes API, and Spark then creates and owns the executors. Local routes use your Kubernetes credentials; remote submission uses the API's service account after its policy admits the job. The API is optional: it adds a browser console, proxies and policy-gated remote submission on top of the same client.

docs.title: Before you rely on it
docs.text:
The develop documentation follows main. Before copying its examples, choose a matching published release or a source installation. Installing the PyPI package does not include the repository's example files. Chart and package releases are independent. Read support boundaries before planning production operation: this project does not provide a multi-tenant scheduler, a highly available metadata service or an embedded identity provider.

Contributors can use the repository map and check routes. Maintainers use the release runbook to qualify and publish artifacts.

docs.title: Development and validation
docs.text: This is the canonical check guide for contributors and repository agents. Commands run from the repository root unless stated otherwise. Workflow files define the current CI matrices; adjust this guide when those files change.

docs.title: Structure and contracts
docs.text:
Area Implementation Checks and docs Submission and lifecycle client.py, utils/, k8s/ under spark_on_k8s/ tests/test_spark_client.py, tests/utils/, tests/k8s/, tests/integration/spark/ Documents and plans jobs.py, planning.py, cli/job.py tests/test_jobs.py, tests/cli/, job files CLI and SQL cli/, sql/ tests/cli/, tests/sql/, automation, SQL API, policy and proxies api/, remote.py tests/api/, remote submission Airflow airflow/ tests/airflow/, Airflow Shared console frontend/src/ frontend/tests/; both Python static asset trees Diagnostics and recorder diagnostics.py, doctor.py, history/ tests/test_diagnostics.py, tests/history/, diagnostics, history Packaging and deployment pyproject.toml, uv.lock, docker/, chart/ tests/chart/, built wheel checks, releases

Keep UI behavior in shared components; host entry points only supply transports and context. Preserve machine-readable schemas and exit codes separately from human messages. Treat active, absent, terminal and unknown outcomes as different states. See support boundaries before adding a public contract.

docs.title: Choose checks by change
docs.text:
Touched behavior Minimum relevant route before PR Documentation prose, links or agent instructions Strict docs build; validate edited skills; no runtime matrix solely for prose Core, CLI, SQL or offline planning Focused regression tests, core/API profile and Ruff; installed wheel if packaging/import behavior changes Submission, wait, retry, cancel or cleanup Relevant unit profiles plus real Spark Kubernetes workflow; Airflow Kubernetes workflow for operator/trigger lifecycle changes Airflow or provider packaging Installed-wheel Airflow 3 and 2.11 profiles; native task UI backend checks on Airflow 3 API/remote/proxy behavior tests/api/ and relevant CLI tests; browser checks when browser transports or URLs change Frontend Format, build, both packaged asset trees and browser tests; relevant API/Airflow backend tests Helm tests/chart/ with Helm installed; regenerate chart documentation and strict docs build Dependencies/build/release Lock check, applicable installed-wheel profiles, package build and affected runtime workflows Connect tests/test_connect.py plus real Connect workflow for client/protocol changes Jupyter example or helper Exact notebook kernel/Kubernetes runner in the Connect workflow, helper failure-path checks, strict docs and download parity Experimental dbt adapter Separate locked profile, installed plugin/core wheels, lifecycle/cursor tests and both Kubernetes transport jobs Starter/example runtime Its output assertions in the advertised runtime; extend the corresponding workflow when support claims change

Do not run every expensive matrix locally for a small change. Do not omit a relevant runtime requirement because its unit tests pass. Use CI for unavailable Docker, Kubernetes or alternate interpreters and record the pending check. Once checks pass, repeat them only after relevant changes or newly discovered risks.

docs.title: Python profiles
docs.text:
Use Python 3.11+ and uv 0.13.7, matching CI. Keep uv.lock committed. Profiles below use separate environments so concurrent checks do not replace each other's packages. The test group is otherwise selected by default.

Core/API (CI covers Python 3.11–3.15, plus selected macOS ARM64 combinations):

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=.venv-core uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --group test --extra api --extra sql
.venv-core/bin/python -m pytest tests --ignore=tests/airflow

Pass a test path or -k expression for the initial focused run. Install Helm for chart tests. The CI profile requires collected tests and rejects skips; unavailable tools are not a passing result.

A virtual environment isolates Python packages, but not Airflow's default home, configuration or metadata database. Each profile below uses its own fresh scratch AIRFLOW_HOME and AIRFLOW_CONFIG inside a subshell, before importing Airflow. This avoids Airflow 2 reading settings written by Airflow 3 (such as its XCom backend) and leaves the user's existing Airflow configuration untouched. Keep these settings on focused reruns too; do not copy one version's configuration into the other profile. Scratch homes remain available for inspecting failed runs.

Airflow 3 (CI selects 3.4.0 on Python 3.11–3.14; use only airflow-ui so the standalone API extra cannot hide a missing native-UI dependency):

(
  export AIRFLOW_HOME="$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/spark-airflow3.XXXXXX")"
  export AIRFLOW_CONFIG="$AIRFLOW_HOME/airflow.cfg"
  UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=.venv-airflow3 uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --group test --extra airflow-ui
  uv build --wheel
  uv pip install --python .venv-airflow3/bin/python --no-deps --reinstall dist/*.whl
  .venv-airflow3/bin/python -I tests/run_installed_tests.py tests/airflow
  uv pip check --python .venv-airflow3/bin/python
)

Airflow 2.11.2 uses a fresh separate environment on Python 3.11 or 3.12 (the CI legacy row uses 3.12). Never downgrade an Airflow 3 environment: its separate core/task-SDK packages can remain installed.

(
  export AIRFLOW_HOME="$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/spark-airflow211.XXXXXX")"
  export AIRFLOW_CONFIG="$AIRFLOW_HOME/airflow.cfg"
  UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=.venv-airflow211 uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --group test
  uv pip install --python .venv-airflow211/bin/python '.[airflow]' 'apache-airflow==2.11.2'
  .venv-airflow211/bin/python -c 'import airflow; assert airflow.__version__ == "2.11.2"'
  uv build --wheel
  uv pip install --python .venv-airflow211/bin/python --no-deps --reinstall dist/*.whl
  .venv-airflow211/bin/python -I tests/run_installed_tests.py tests/airflow --ignore=tests/airflow/ui
  uv pip check --python .venv-airflow211/bin/python
)

Use the environment's Python directly after installing the wheel or legacy override: uv run/uv sync can restore the editable project or locked Airflow 3. Exclude only the native UI suite from Airflow 2; remaining profile tests must run without skips. CI also verifies interpreter versions, provider discovery, lazy plugin registration, packaged assets and absence of unintended API imports.

For core packaging changes, build and install the wheel into .venv-core with uv pip install --python .venv-core/bin/python --no-deps --reinstall dist/*.whl, then run .venv-core/bin/python -I tests/run_installed_tests.py tests --ignore=tests/airflow. The runner rejects editable installations and imports outside the environment. Use a fresh build output directory or remove only known stale build outputs before using dist/*.whl; it must identify exactly the wheel under review.

docs.title: Formatting, packaging and documentation
docs.text:
UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=.venv-quality uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --group lint --group docs --all-extras
.venv-quality/bin/ruff check .
.venv-quality/bin/ruff format --check .
.venv-quality/bin/sqlfluff lint examples/airflow
uv lock --check
uv build
.venv-quality/bin/helm-mkdocs chart -o docs/helm-chart
.venv-quality/bin/mkdocs build --strict
.venv-quality/bin/python scripts/check_docs.py site

For prose-only edits, the last three commands are sufficient once the documentation environment exists. The full site generates Python API reference pages, so its build environment needs the documented extras even when the prose itself does not exercise them. Generated chart docs and site/ are ignored outputs; do not commit them. The offline link check also validates generated HTML anchors and local assets; external sites and version-switcher destinations need a published-site review. Keep instructions canonical and link them from the README rather than maintaining additional command copies.

A user-visible change also adds its PR link to the planned file in release-notes/ when one exists, under the matching section. Published release bodies are historical records; see release notes before editing one. python scripts/release_notes.py check validates the files without building the site.

Repository skills are small Markdown packages. If the installed skill-creator validator is available, run its scripts/quick_validate.py against each edited folder in .agents/skills/. Also read every relative reference and dry-run a representative task without publication: syntactic validation does not establish that a release skill respects authorization or selects the correct tests.

docs.title: Shared frontend
docs.text:
Use Node.js 26 and the committed npm lockfile. From frontend/:

npm ci
npm run format:check
npm run build
npx playwright install chromium
npm test

npm run build checks TypeScript and regenerates both spark_on_k8s/api/webserver/static/ui and spark_on_k8s/airflow/ui/static. Commit both asset sets and license notices with source changes. CI rebuilds and rejects stale or untracked assets. Fixtures use mocked services and are not packaged in the wheel. A passing fixture test is not a browser-to-cluster test. npm run dev serves fixtures; npm run test:ui opens the interactive test runner. For the packaged app, start the API as documented and open /webserver/apps, respecting its configured URL prefix.

docs.title: Real runtime checks
docs.text:
Use only a disposable, explicitly selected kind cluster. The workflow setup pins images/tooling, installs a built wheel, creates its own test resources, applies bounded deadlines and uploads diagnostics before cleanup. Never point these tests at an arbitrary current kubeconfig context.

  • .github/workflows/spark-compatibility.yml runs tests/integration/spark/run_kubernetes.py. Use its image-building and kind setup steps, then pass --kubeconfig, --context, --image, --spark-version and --artifacts as specified by the runner. It covers real Python, SQL, failure and Java submissions, executor ownership and resource cleanup. Changes to lifecycle behavior extend this harness instead of adding a second client harness.
  • .github/workflows/airflow-kubernetes.yml runs tests/integration/airflow/run_kubernetes.py against Airflow 2.11.2 and 3.4.0 on Python 3.12 with one representative Spark 4.0.5 image. Six cases cover success, executor-backed application failure and Pending/Unschedulable startup timeout, each synchronously and with real deferred-task resumption. The runner uses DAG.test() in a Kubernetes pod with real database/XCom/inline triggers; this does not exercise a deployed scheduler, separate triggerer process, worker crash or durable reattachment after XCom clearing. Retained-XCom adoption failures remain covered by operator regression tests.
  • .github/workflows/spark-connect.yml runs tests/integration/connect/run.py against a separate local Spark Connect server for client compatibility. Its Kubernetes job additionally creates Spark 4.0.5/4.3.0 servers with real executors and exercises SDK/CLI receipts, query readiness, session independence, failure handling and ownership-safe deletion using tests/integration/connect/run_kubernetes.py. The same image matrix runs tests/integration/jupyter/run_kubernetes.py, executing the canonical examples/jupyter/spark_connect.ipynb with a real IPython kernel. It performs a planned kernel restart, reconnects to the same driver, verifies distributed results and notebook table output, then observes owned cleanup. This covers kernel execution, not manual JupyterLab browser interaction or an abrupt kernel/driver crash. Use the locked notebook group plus connect extra in its isolated Python 3.12 environment; the workflow installs the built wheel. Each Kubernetes row intentionally overrides the locked thin client with uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps "pyspark-client==$SPARK_VERSION", then runs uv pip check, pairing clients and servers at 4.0.5 and 4.3.0. Run the environment's Python directly after that override: a subsequent sync can restore the locked client or editable package. Preserve the notebook's local-row DataFrame case; passing range queries alone does not establish that newer client APIs work against an older server. The notebook writes notebook-result.json; the runner publishes aggregate result.json after fixture and tunnel cleanup, so passing cells alone do not establish a passing integration run. Keep the executed notebook and cleanup evidence with the result. The Jupyter guide documents interactive use.
  • tests/integration/starters/check.py verifies ETL/Iceberg output and replay in the selected Spark image. Its container-local results do not validate shared storage provisioning on a target cluster.

After the Airflow workflow's wheel/image build and disposable-cluster setup, its host command is:

.venv/bin/python -I tests/integration/airflow/run_kubernetes.py \
  --kubeconfig "$RUNNER_TEMP/airflow-kubeconfig" --context kind-airflow-compat \
  --airflow-image "airflow-compat:$AIRFLOW_VERSION" --airflow-version "$AIRFLOW_VERSION" \
  --spark-image airflow-spark:4.0.5 --spark-version 4.0.5 \
  --artifacts "$RUNNER_TEMP/airflow-kubernetes-results"

A valid result includes result.json with all six cases passed, the Airflow log, Kubernetes pod/event/log evidence and kind logs. See the harness boundary before claiming broader scheduler coverage.

Release helpers have focused offline tests in tests/release/: python -m pytest tests/release. Packaging-related PRs also build a nonpublishing preview in .github/workflows/release.yml; actual release eligibility is a separate exact-commit gate. See the dry-run procedure.

The Spark compatibility guide describes the selected version matrix and local Spark fallback. Local mode is useful additional evidence but does not validate Kubernetes RBAC, pod networking or garbage collection. Record workflow URL, tested commit, scenario results and any omitted environment in PR/release validation. A failed or unexecuted scenario is not coverage.

docs.title: Experimental dbt integration
docs.text:
integrations/dbt/ is a separate Python distribution with its own lockfile. Its dbt.adapters.spark_on_k8s namespace reuses upstream Spark macros; the spark_on_k8s_dbt package owns the full command lifecycle. Changes to either must keep server ownership independent from dbt's intermediate connection cleanup.

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT="$PWD/.venv-dbt" uv sync \
  --project integrations/dbt --locked --python 3.12 --group test
uv build --wheel --out-dir dist/dbt-check
uv build --project integrations/dbt --wheel --out-dir dist/dbt-check
uv pip install --python .venv-dbt/bin/python --no-deps --reinstall dist/dbt-check/*.whl
.venv-dbt/bin/python -I -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider integrations/dbt/tests
uv pip check --python .venv-dbt/bin/python

Use tests/integration/dbt/run_kubernetes.py as documented in that directory's README for real runtime checks. The Experimental managed dbt workflow installs both wheels and tests Thrift and Connect separately on Spark 4.3.0/Python 3.12, with fixtures and cleanup evidence. A mock test or receipt alone does not prove SQL execution, table persistence or resource disappearance. Keep the published profile and command guide synchronized with this runner.

docs.title: Release runbook
docs.text: Use this runbook to prepare a release or to publish one when the user/maintainer has explicitly authorized publication. Preparing notes, local checks and an artifact record does not publish; the documented dry-run workflow performs hosted validation without publishing. Pushing a version tag starts external publication. Reuse authorization already given for the concrete release. Do not ask again merely because this page contains a publication checkpoint.

docs.title: Observed practice and its evidence
docs.text:
The following historical sources were inspected on 7 November 2026. They establish naming and communication patterns, not proof that every historical release ran present-day checks.

Evidence What it establishes 0.12.1, 7 April 2025 Bare numeric tag, title Spark On K8S 0.12.1, grouped fixes/miscellaneous changes, PR links and a full comparison link; documentation versioning is listed as a change 0.12.0, 17 February 2025 Fixes, features and maintenance changes are grouped and linked to their PRs 0.11.0, 19 January 2025 Python 3.8 support removal is called out as a significant change Discussion 127 A concrete UI configuration request received a maintainer reply linking PR 132 and the new settings, subsequently listed in 0.12.0 Discussion 124 A usage request led to published driver examples; the maintainer explicitly noted the then-current main-branch docs and planned versioning Discussion 72 Packaging guidance favored including Python modules in the application image, with alternatives described rather than a new deployment system

These discussions are user support evidence. They do not establish a mandatory release announcement, voting process or permission to post a new message. Source links in release notes should connect a change to its real PR/discussion; do not describe analytical review personas as customer feedback.

The current repository workflows are the source of truth for mechanics:

  • .github/workflows/release.yml: tag-triggered Python distributions, PyPI and API image publication. The release build sets the package version from the tag.
  • .github/workflows/deploy-doc.yml: main publishes develop; a qualified tag publishes that documentation version. Only the highest stable numeric version can update the latest alias.
  • .github/workflows/helm-release.yml: independent manual dispatch with app_version and chart_version, publishing to the chart repository. It rejects an unpublished or pre-/ready API image and an already published chart version before packaging.

Read these files at the candidate commit before acting. Existing release tags can be newer than the development version string in pyproject.toml (the inspected source had 0.11.0-dev while historical releases include 0.12.1). Never select the next version by incrementing that development string alone.

docs.title: Packages and release order
docs.text:
One project release can involve up to four independently versioned artifacts. They are published by different workflows and must not be forced to share a number:

Artifact Version source Publication Depends on spark-on-k8s wheel/sdist and API image Bare X.Y.Z tag release.yml on the tag push Exact qualified commit Versioned documentation Same tag deploy-doc.yml on the tag push Same eligibility record Helm chart chart_version input; appVersion from app_version Manual helm-release.yml Published API image for app_version Experimental dbt-spark-on-k8s integrations/dbt/pyproject.toml Not automated yet Published spark-on-k8s on PyPI

Publish in that order. The chart's default image tag is its appVersion, so releasing the chart before the matching API image exists produces an install that cannot pull its image. The dbt adapter's metadata must name a released SDK version, which only exists after the package upload. Record a chart or adapter that is intentionally not released with the package as such, rather than leaving it implied.

docs.title: Release notes
docs.text:
Canonical release notes live in release-notes/X.Y.Z.md, one file per GitHub release. Each file contains YAML metadata followed by the exact GitHub release body:

---
version: "0.13.0"
title: "Spark On K8S 0.13.0"
date: null
status: "planned"
github_url: "https://github.com/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s/releases/tag/0.13.0"
---

Release body …

scripts/release_notes.py check validates the metadata, filename/version match and LF line endings, and rejects a planned release older than the newest published one. Bodies of releases published before this page existed were copied from GitHub without rewording. Draft the next release as status: "planned" while changes merge; keep significant/migration changes first, then features, fixes, other packages, maintenance, contributors and the exact comparison link.

The release-notes page is a separate small site shared by every documentation version, and every version's navigation links to that permanent URL. Main-branch documentation deployments rebuild it from release-notes/*.md and commit it to gh-pages under release-notes/; tag deployments leave it untouched, so publishing an older maintenance release cannot replace newer history. It is not a mike version and does not appear in the version selector. Planned releases are labeled In preparation, and their documentation and comparison links open the develop documentation and a comparison with main until the release exists. Preview it locally with:

.venv-quality/bin/python scripts/release_notes.py build --output-dir release-notes-site
.venv-quality/bin/python scripts/check_docs.py release-notes-site

When publishing, export the reviewed body instead of maintaining a second copy. Extraction only writes a local file:

.venv-quality/bin/python scripts/release_notes.py extract "$RELEASE_VERSION" \
  --output "/tmp/spark-on-k8s-$RELEASE_VERSION-notes.md"

After the package and GitHub release are confirmed, set the file's status to published and its date to the GitHub publication date in a signed documentation PR. Its main deployment updates the shared page without rebuilding archived version documentation. Correct historical bodies only deliberately, and edit the GitHub release in the same change so the two stay identical.

docs.title: Separate experimental dbt distribution
docs.text: integrations/dbt is an opt-in experiment with an independent version and lockfile. The main release workflow builds and publishes the root package only; it does not publish dbt-spark-on-k8s. The experimental package currently pins the development SDK from the same checkout. Before changing that pin or publishing the experiment, select the actual compatible SDK artifact, update its lockfile, and run both transport jobs in dbt-kubernetes.yml against the proposed pair. A normal root release does not establish compatibility for a separately rebuilt adapter.

docs.title: Current safeguards
docs.text: Signed commits, explicit tested-commit evidence, compatibility notes and an artifact record below are requirements of this contributor workflow. They are stated here as current safeguards, not inferred historical practice. Automated gates should implement the same checks; do not treat a documented manual check as an enforced GitHub rule. Inspect existing repository/environment controls before adding a redundant gate.

docs.title: Implementation and dry-run
docs.text:
scripts/release_eligibility.py validates a bare X.Y.Z version (optionally aN, bN or rcN) and requires successful runs of ci.yml, spark-compatibility.yml, spark-connect.yml and airflow-kubernetes.yml for the exact commit. Only same-repository push/manual runs qualify; PR runs and another commit's green results do not. The latest eligible run must pass every job: empty or skipped execution fails closed. Missing/in-progress runs are polled for up to 30 minutes by the workflow; failures, API errors or expiry stop publication. The CLI accepts a bounded 1–3600 second budget for independent checks.

For a local read-only eligibility check, set RELEASE_VERSION to the reviewed candidate version and provide an existing read-only Actions credential through GH_TOKEN, then run:

CANDIDATE_SHA="$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
python scripts/release_eligibility.py \
  --repository hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s --commit "$CANDIDATE_SHA" \
  --version "$RELEASE_VERSION" --timeout-seconds 300 \
  --output /tmp/spark-release-eligibility.json

For the release workflow's manual Run workflow, choose the candidate branch or tag in GitHub's native ref selector and supply the version input. Every job checks out the resulting immutable event SHA; there is no arbitrary checkout-ref input. This path runs eligibility, builds distributions and tests frozen API images for Linux amd64 and arm64, then stops before PyPI/registry publication. It does not trigger a documentation push. Qualify missing main-commit workflows via their own manual runs first; the core CI dispatch runs all profiles even for a documentation-only candidate.

Packaging-related PRs run the same artifact/container path with preview version 0.0.0rc1 and read-only permissions. They intentionally skip release eligibility: PR image validation does not claim that the future merge commit passed main checks. Both publishing jobs are restricted to tag-push events. Preview artifacts must not be used as released packages.

scripts/release_artifacts.py prepare rejects ambiguous build directories and mismatched wheel/sdist versions. The workflow exports the API-only dependency closure from uv.lock before substituting the release version. The API Dockerfile installs the actual wheel plus hash-checked binary dependencies from that export; it no longer resolves the project version from PyPI. Generated build inputs live under docker/release/ and must not be committed. Their manifest records source SHA, wheel/sdist hashes, lock/requirements hashes, pinned base reference and the actual bundled frontend components from the wheel's license notices. Airflow's host-supplied React is not counted as a bundled dependency. Each architecture records installed Python packages at /opt/spark-on-k8s/release/installed.json.

The release-eligibility, release-container-inputs, release-installed-* and published-release-manifest workflow artifacts contain these records. Registry publication rebuilds from the same frozen inputs; it does not promote the exact image digest used in the architecture checks and does not promise bit-for-bit reproducibility. It also requests the build action's OCI SBOM and provenance attestations. Attach the relevant manifest and qualification links to the GitHub release for retention beyond transient workflow artifacts. A generated inventory or SBOM is not a certification that dependencies are vulnerability-free.

New tag-publication runs are serialized. The gate compares all existing bare stable numeric tags: only a highest stable version may move global latest, and only a highest version within a minor may move its major.minor image tag. Prereleases move neither. Documentation uses the same global rule. Thus a later 0.12.2 maintenance release does not overwrite latest after 0.13.0. A higher failed tag conservatively prevents lower-version promotion; resolve that state explicitly instead of automatically moving channels backward. GHCR's destination uses the repository owner, independently of the person rerunning the workflow.

docs.title: Documentation publication
docs.text:
The docs workflow adds its isolated environment to PATH because mike launches its documentation builder as a child command. mike deploy builds once using the strict configuration, updates only the local gh-pages branch, and records the source SHA and channel in versions.json. The generated HTML must pass the local link, anchor and asset check before that branch is pushed. The checked site is retained as the documentation-site workflow artifact.

Every newly built page labels its channel: develop is unreleased main-branch content; a prerelease names its candidate version; a release names its exact tag. The source link identifies the immutable commit used for that build. Local builds without publication metadata say Local documentation preview. Existing archived versions are preserved and may predate these labels. The version selector and latest alias describe documentation versions, not the package installed in a reader's environment. Page revision dates describe source edits, not the last successful deployment.

After a docs deployment, verify the public develop/ or versioned homepage, its source link and versions.json against the workflow commit. Check latest/ only when the release is eligible to advance that alias. A failed publishing run can leave older pages publicly available; a successful local build alone does not prove the public site has updated. Diagnose the failed run before retrying, and never treat an old page's content or timestamp as evidence for the new commit.

docs.title: 1. Establish the candidate
docs.text:
Record the intended version, full commit SHA, previous published tag and intended release type. Inspect local changes, repository identity, remotes and current published tags/releases. Use the actual configured remote or explicit repository URL; do not assume that origin exists. Confirm the candidate contains the intended merged changes, and that the version is unused. Do not guess a release number when it has not been selected by the maintainer.

Compare from the previous actual release, not from an arbitrary development version. Prepare notes in release-notes/X.Y.Z.md as described in Release notes: significant/migration changes first, then features, fixes, other packages, maintenance, contributors where applicable, and the exact comparison link. Include support retirements, changed defaults and operational limitations. The planned file is a reviewable draft; merging it does not publish a release.

docs.title: 2. Qualify the exact commit and artifacts
docs.text:
Use development validation. For a release candidate, require:

  • Locked dependencies; lint, format, strict docs and clean package builds.
  • Core/API CI across the supported Python matrix and installed-wheel checks.
  • Installed-wheel provider/operator checks for both Airflow 3 and 2.11, including lazy discovery and Airflow 3's native task UI with only its own extra installed.
  • Shared frontend build/browser checks and clean regenerated packaged assets.
  • Real Spark Kubernetes and Airflow Kubernetes scenarios for the selected candidate; the real Connect workflow when that integration is included in the release. Preserve the workflow URLs, commit SHA and scenario artifacts.
  • Verification that distribution metadata equals the selected release version, and that container inputs use the release wheel and intended dependency/base inputs.

Required evidence must match the exact commit that will be tagged. A green check on a PR head does not prove the merge commit passed. Path-filtered workflows can have no run on a docs-only merge; run the missing qualification on the candidate when publication requires it. A successful workflow with skipped required scenarios is insufficient. If infrastructure is unavailable locally, use hosted disposable jobs and wait for their results; never substitute mocked or local-mode results for Kubernetes evidence.

Build the release-version candidate in an isolated checkout/output directory when the development version differs. Keep the working development checkout intact. Record which built artifacts were actually tested; a source checkout test does not validate a wheel. The release workflow must fail before publishing on missing or failed eligibility evidence, version mismatch or artifact validation failure.

docs.title: 3. Review identity, notes and authorization
docs.text:
Verify signed commits using the contributor's configured trust setup. Do not disable signing, impersonate a maintainer or replace signing identity to get past a failure. Resolve unknown-key verification separately from an invalid signature. Use a signed annotated version tag for a newly published release and verify its signature before pushing. These are current safeguards; they are not claims about all historical tags.

At this checkpoint the candidate SHA/version, passing evidence, release notes and artifact destinations must be concrete. If the request was preparation only, return those materials and stop before a tag push, release publication or publishing workflow dispatch. The explicitly nonpublishing validation path above remains available. If publication of this release was already authorized, proceed within that authorization. Do not publish a discussion or contact contributors without explicit authorization for that communication.

docs.title: 4. Publish through the existing channels
docs.text:
Push only the intended verified version tag to the inspected repository. Tags trigger package/image and documentation publication; monitor all relevant runs. Before a prerelease or maintenance release, inspect the eligibility record's promote_latest and promote_minor decisions and establish the intended destinations. The version itself can publish without advancing either mutable channel.

Publish the GitHub release against that tag with the body extracted from its release-notes file, without creating a second tag at a different commit. For example, gh release create "$RELEASE_VERSION" --verify-tag --title "Spark On K8S $RELEASE_VERSION" --notes-file "/tmp/spark-on-k8s-$RELEASE_VERSION-notes.md". Publish an updated chart only when requested and needed, after the matching API image exists, using the independent workflow's explicit app/chart versions. Do not force all channels to increment together. Do not dispatch a workflow from a different default-branch commit while claiming it validated the tagged candidate.

docs.title: 5. Verify and record the usable combination
docs.text:
Resolve published artifacts and retain a small release record containing:

Field Required evidence Source/package Full source commit, tag, package version and wheel/sdist hashes API image Registry references and immutable digests; base/dependency inventory where produced Chart Actual chart version and app version, or explicitly not released/qualified Documentation Version URL and source revision Validation Exact workflow runs, scenario outcomes and limits of validation

For a recommended API deployment, render the selected chart with the exact image reference and record the settings used. Claim a cluster-qualified combination only after that exact image/chart combination passes a staging smoke test; otherwise label it render/package validation. Historical releases without such a record are not retroactively certified. Link installation instructions to the recorded version, not mutable latest or main-branch examples.

If a stage fails, preserve successful artifacts, inspect the failed stage, and retry only a safe, understood operation. Do not delete/reuse a published version, move a published tag, or repeatedly upload an immutable package. A correction may need a new patch release. Document partial publication and resolve it before claiming the release complete.

docs.title: Review decisions
docs.text:
This records the disposition of all 100 proposals, 50 feedback notes and 50 scope cautions from the November 2026 review. The proposals are analytical suggestions, not customer demand. Repeated ideas share one implementation. A decision is not a claim that every suggested feature was built.

Concrete correctness and usability findings are fixed or documented in the linked changes. Broader integration proposals remain uncommitted candidates with explicit acceptance criteria. Cloud-account, GPU, multi-tenant authorization and new control-plane support are not implied by configuration examples.

The maintained roadmap is TODO. Use development checks and support boundaries before promoting a candidate to supported functionality.

docs.title: 01.1 · A copyable Python project packaging recipe with executor import checks
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. The existing ETL path and first-run route are maintained; additional Python packaging/parity starters need a concrete application and runtime acceptance fixture.

Required evidence before implementation: From a clean checkout and a prepared cluster, an engineer can replace the helper with a two-module project and complete the documented import check within 30 minutes; a deliberately missing executor dependency produces a failing check.

docs.title: 01.2 · A pandas-to-Spark migration walkthrough with output parity
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. The existing ETL path and first-run route are maintained; additional Python packaging/parity starters need a concrete application and runtime acceptance fixture.

Required evidence before implementation: The documented command proves matching clean orders, quarantine reasons, and revenue on the fixture; changing one date or deduplication rule makes the parity comparison fail with a useful row difference.

Feedback: Put the existing verified ETL path before placeholder submission. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid turning submit into implicit environment deployment. Automatically uploading the current virtual environment or installing arbitrary packages at startup would blur an understandable image boundary and create slow, hard-to-reproduce failures. A small, checked packaging recipe serves this persona with less ongoing maintenance.

docs.title: 02.1 · Check an explicit JVM build/runtime compatibility descriptor
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. JVM compatibility is qualified explicitly; another descriptor/starter should be driven by a real Java/Scala application and connector set.

Required evidence before implementation: A matching fixture passes; Scala 2.12 declared against a 2.13 runtime fails before any Kubernetes call; missing runtime metadata produces an explicit unknown result. Existing jobs remain usable without this optional check.

docs.title: 02.2 · Add one reproducible JVM dependency-packaging starter
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. JVM compatibility is qualified explicitly; another descriptor/starter should be driven by a real Java/Scala application and connector set.

Required evidence before implementation: The image completes a distributed check while runtime artifact-repository access is unavailable. Artifact inspection confirms the helper dependency is present and Spark implementation classes are excluded. Rebuilding from identical declared inputs yields the same dependency inventory.

Feedback: Keep JVM compatibility claims tied to the tested workload. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid a separate Java/Scala submission SDK. Image-local jars, class entrypoints, declarative jobs, and the CLI already provide a language-neutral deployment boundary. Another SDK adds release obligations without directly solving artifact reproducibility. Validate adoption friction before expanding that surface.

docs.title: 03.1 · Include a verified cluster target in diagnostic receipts
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Production deployment inputs are documented now; cluster fleet context and maintenance presets need a selected operational environment.

Required evidence before implementation: Run the same namespace/service-account check against two test contexts and confirm saved reports remain distinguishable without shell history. Cover in-cluster and custom-client paths, missing context metadata, endpoint redaction, and JSON compatibility. Never export credentials or kubeconfig contents.

docs.title: 03.2 · Provide an explicit maintenance and disruption profile for the API chart
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Production deployment inputs are documented now; cluster fleet context and maintenance presets need a selected operational environment.

Required evidence before implementation: A chart rendering matrix covers defaults and both maintenance profiles. A documented drain/upgrade exercise measures readiness transitions, completed requests, interruption duration, and reconnect behavior. The history example states its measured outage instead of promising zero downtime.

Feedback: Make production release identity and resource assumptions visible. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid building a central fleet scheduler. Cluster federation, capacity balancing, and cross-cluster failover multiply credentials, state, and recovery obligations. Target-aware reports and operational deployment examples offer useful SRE improvements while keeping each existing deployment independently understandable.

docs.title: 04.1 · Fail safely when retry attachment cannot be verified
docs.text: Implemented. Uncertain Airflow lookup now propagates instead of resubmitting; 404 alone establishes absence. Implementation or contract.

docs.title: 04.2 · Template package coordinates and pod attribution consistently
docs.text:
Implemented. Packages and pod labels/annotations participate in Airflow templating, with both-version tests. Implementation or contract.

Feedback: Explain lifecycle policies with a scheduled-task example. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid a second retry and scheduling engine inside the operator. Keep scheduling, backfills, task concurrency, and retry timing in Airflow. Improve attachment decisions and expose Spark lifecycle facts without adding hidden resubmission loops that make hundreds of scheduled tasks harder to reason about. Application-level idempotent output handling remains necessary.

docs.title: 05.1 · Add an Airflow component preflight using the actual Kubernetes connection
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Permissions are clarified; component preflight and a multi-backend registry add deployment contracts that need a real Airflow installation.

Required evidence before implementation: In supported Airflow environments, a missing triggerer kubeconfig and a denied pod-read permission produce distinct actionable findings within 30 seconds; healthy worker and triggerer checks pass without creating persistent Kubernetes objects or exposing connection secrets.

docs.title: 05.2 · Allow an administrator-defined registry of task UI backends
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Permissions are clarified; component preflight and a multi-backend registry add deployment contracts that need a real Airflow installation.

Required evidence before implementation: Two tasks using two registered clusters display their respective applications even when namespace and pod names coincide; unknown backend identifiers fail closed, and writes stay disabled for the read-only backend.

Feedback: Document submission privileges separately from task-tab permissions. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid inventing a parallel Airflow identity and secrets system. Continue using KubernetesHook, AsyncKubernetesHook, existing Airflow connections, and Airflow authorization. A bespoke connection type or credential store would increase upgrade and rotation work without addressing the observed component-readiness or single-backend gaps. UI permissions must not be marketed as isolation for arbitrary DAG code.

docs.title: 06.1 · Locate failed SQL statements by file and line
docs.text: Partially implemented. SQL source basename, statement and line are preserved; failure logging avoids full query text. Structured execution events/timing and a completed/unstarted summary remain candidates. Implementation or contract.

docs.title: 06.2 · Typed run-date parameters for repeatable SQL jobs
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Source-aware failures are delivered first. Typed SQL parameters require Spark-version-specific semantics and a separate injection-safe API design.

Required evidence before implementation: Run one unchanged SQL file against two dates and verify only the intended partitions are addressed. An apostrophe-containing string remains one literal; unresolved placeholders and invalid dates fail locally before Kubernetes resources are created.

Feedback: Make query previews a deliberate production choice. Query text is no longer logged by the wrapper, and result-row exposure is documented. A quiet preview mode is not added because skipping a Spark action could change execution semantics; it requires a separate tested design. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid automatic resume from the failed statement. Earlier statements may already have committed writes, while temporary views belong to the prior session. Skipping earlier statements or replaying them blindly can both change results. Keep recovery explicit until a workload supplies a verifiable idempotency contract. A statement summary helps an analyst decide; it does not establish safe retry boundaries.

docs.title: 07.1 · Publish a multi-cell notebook session lifecycle recipe
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Generated-data onboarding is corrected; session lifecycle/transfer recipes need a chosen notebook and server configuration.

Required evidence before implementation: Execute the example cells in order and rerun setup twice: temporary views survive between analysis cells, each replaced session is closed once, final cleanup is safe to repeat, and another independent client remains usable. A new user can complete it using only a supplied profile and credentials.

docs.title: 07.2 · Extend the Connect check with an opt-in notebook data-transfer check
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Generated-data onboarding is corrected; session lifecycle/transfer recipes need a chosen notebook and server configuration.

Required evidence before implementation: The notebook mode passes against the existing integration server, reports a distinct sanitized conversion failure when conversion is deliberately broken, respects the same total timeout, and exposes no tokens or data paths. The default check retains its present behavior.

Feedback: Make the first notebook example independent of a private warehouse. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid turning notebook convenience into automatic infrastructure ownership. Do not launch shared servers, request Kubernetes access, or upload arbitrary local notebook directories as a convenience default. Endpoint provisioning and storage authorization are platform responsibilities; keep improvements centered on a supplied profile, bounded synthetic checks, and explicit session ownership.

docs.title: 08.1 · Add a reproducible batch-inference starter with an application-owned manifest
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. ML adaptation limitations are documented. GPU/inference examples need hardware, a model artifact and an owner for recurring executor tests.

Required evidence before implementation: Two executions against the same fixture and model produce identical sorted predictions and identity fields; changing the expected model digest fails before outputs are published; changing the input identifier is visible in the manifest.

docs.title: 08.2 · Document and validate a CPU-driver, accelerator-executor inference recipe
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. ML adaptation limitations are documented. GPU/inference examples need hardware, a model artifact and an owner for recurring executor tests.

Required evidence before implementation: Offline fixtures flag each documented contradiction and accept the reference profile. Before declaring runtime support, an opt-in accelerator-cluster smoke test verifies an executor uses the device while the driver requests none.

Feedback: Mark the latest-event ETL example as unsuitable for historical feature reconstruction. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid turning submission tooling into a feature store or model lifecycle platform. Registry promotion, feature serving, experiment tracking, and training orchestration create unrelated state and support obligations. Prefer small reproducible applications and explicit integration contracts; build further ML features only after actual adoption evidence.

docs.title: 09.1 · Ship a checkpoint-preserving streaming restart starter
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Termination semantics are clarified. Checkpoint/freshness recipes need a real source, sink and recovery contract.

Required evidence before implementation: Process a deterministic sequence of input files, stop and redeploy with the same checkpoint, add more files, and assert the expected output set without rereading committed input in this specific example. Repeat after abrupt driver loss. An operator following the recipe can identify the checkpoint and confirm there is only one active driver before resubmission.

docs.title: 09.2 · Add an opt-in streaming progress and freshness integration recipe
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Termination semantics are clarified. Checkpoint/freshness recipes need a real source, sink and recovery contract.

Required evidence before implementation: A demonstration distinguishes normal processing, healthy idle input, delayed processing, terminated query with a still-live process, and missing telemetry. A stopped instrumentation feed becomes unknown/stale within the configured freshness threshold, without turning an idle stream into a failure.

Feedback: Describe kill as a termination request, not a completed drain. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid automatic restarts inferred solely from pod phase. A built-in streaming supervisor would add leader election, backoff, upgrade coordination, and checkpoint ownership obligations. Delegate continuous reconciliation to existing orchestration systems; first prove the recovery recipe and query-level observability.

docs.title: 10.1 · Provide a tested REST-catalog and object-storage starter profile
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. The current single-writer Iceberg fixture remains the tested boundary; REST/object-storage and maintenance recipes require a qualified catalog/store.

Required evidence before implementation: An engineer supplies documented endpoints and identity references, then runs the same job through the new profile without editing Python. A separate session reads the expected three orders, a replay preserves their values, and the checked-in manifest contains no credential values.

docs.title: 10.2 · Add an explicit snapshot-retention maintenance recipe
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. The current single-writer Iceberg fixture remains the tested boundary; REST/object-storage and maintenance recipes require a qualified catalog/store.

Required evidence before implementation: On a disposable fixture with several commits, maintenance preserves current rows and the configured protected snapshot while making an intentionally expired snapshot unavailable. The inspection step changes no snapshots; omitting required policy inputs prevents execution.

Feedback: Keep snapshot observations distinct from commit ownership. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Do not turn the submission library into an Iceberg control plane. Catalog hosting, cross-engine writer locking, table governance, and automatic repair would add substantial persistent-state and correctness obligations. Prefer optional recipes and narrowly tested integrations with the catalog and orchestration systems users already operate. A successful Spark run should not be presented as an exactly-once or table-isolation guarantee.

docs.title: 11.1 · Add a narrowly qualified bring-your-own Delta batch recipe
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Map-merge adaptation is documented. Delta support needs a pinned connector/runtime test rather than a compatibility claim from configuration alone.

Required evidence before implementation: From a clean namespace, the documented commands build and submit the example; an independent reader verifies expected keys and values after two replays and reads the earlier version. Report local execution and Kubernetes execution separately.

docs.title: 11.2 · Provide a Delta stream restart qualification recipe
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Map-merge adaptation is documented. Delta support needs a pinned connector/runtime test rather than a compatibility claim from configuration alone.

Required evidence before implementation: Two submissions using the same checkpoint produce exactly the expected fixture keys and counts, preserve the first batch, and include the second. Capture query progress and final table verification so driver completion alone cannot pass the check.

Feedback: Explain profile merge behavior when adapting the Iceberg starter. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid turning submission tooling into a Delta table-management service. Do not add generic optimize, vacuum, protocol-upgrade, or table-repair buttons. Those operations require table-level policies and knowledge of other writers; examples and existing SDK submission preserve the user's established Delta tooling with substantially less support burden. Neither proposal requires owning table lifecycle.

docs.title: 12.1 · Add a Hudi CDC contract starter with ordering and tombstone fixtures
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. CDC ordering/deletion contracts are clarified. Hudi fixtures need a selected source ordering model and recurring table-format tests.

Required evidence before implementation: Execute the fixture twice and in deliberately reordered batches; assert the same final visible rows, source versions, and retained deletion markers. Replay an old insert after deletion and verify it remains invisible. Reject the incompatible schema without changing the table. Run this on one supported dependency combination.

docs.title: 12.2 · Publish a reproducible CDC recovery drill that separates submission from data commit
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. CDC ordering/deletion contracts are clarified. Hudi fixtures need a selected source ordering model and recurring table-format tests.

Required evidence before implementation: For each injected failure, follow the documented commands to recover the same manifest. Verify the checkpoint never skips an uncommitted interval, replay produces the expected table contents, and a changed manifest digest is refused. Demonstrate that missing driver history does not erase the durable recovery evidence.

Feedback: Qualify replay safety by the source ordering contract. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid building a Hudi table-services or CDC connector manager. Owning compaction, cleaning, database log capture, and schema-registry operations would substantially expand the project beyond submitting and observing Spark jobs. Start with one executable integration contract and recovery recipe; leave table lifecycle and source infrastructure with their existing operators.

docs.title: 13.1 · Add an EKS workload-identity and S3 acceptance recipe
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Identity ownership is documented; EKS IAM/storage and executor-loss acceptance require an AWS test account and cost/cleanup boundaries.

Required evidence before implementation: In a disposable EKS namespace, the documented recipe completes a multi-partition S3 round trip with expected row count and no static keys in the job. Removing access to the test prefix makes the check fail visibly. A reviewer can identify the application service account and image dependencies from the saved profile.

docs.title: 13.2 · Provide a mixed-capacity executor-loss rehearsal
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Identity ownership is documented; EKS IAM/storage and executor-loss acceptance require an AWS test account and cost/cleanup boundaries.

Required evidence before implementation: The sample produces the same checksum before and after one executor deletion; the driver remains on its selected pool, replacement execution is visible, and completion stays within an operator-defined recovery budget. A separate deliberate driver-loss run documents the actual terminal behavior rather than implying transparent recovery.

Feedback: Make deployment identity and application identity easier to distinguish. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid becoming an AWS infrastructure and credential manager. Keep IAM provisioning, registry authentication infrastructure, node pools, and interruption handling with existing platform tooling. Versioned examples and acceptance jobs provide AWS adoption value without creating a second cloud control plane or storing credentials in the application service.

docs.title: 14.1 · Publish a keyless GKE-to-GCS acceptance recipe
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Scaling and identity boundaries are documented; GKE storage/elasticity acceptance requires a cloud project and an explicit test owner.

Required evidence before implementation: In a designated GKE acceptance environment, the documented CLI job reads and writes a known dataset from multiple executor partitions with no JSON key mounted and no runtime dependency downloads; checksum and row count match. Removing the bucket grant causes the acceptance job to fail instead of reporting success.

docs.title: 14.2 · Add a GKE Standard elasticity rehearsal profile
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Scaling and identity boundaries are documented; GKE storage/elasticity acceptance requires a cloud project and an explicit test owner.

Required evidence before implementation: With a deliberately capacity-constrained test pool, the second burst produces pending executors, node growth makes them runnable, the job stays within its executor maximum, and idle executors are released. Publish observed timings and node scale-down outcome, including blockers, rather than promising a fixed provisioning latency.

Feedback: Explain the three independent scaling controls together. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid a GCP control-plane subsystem. Do not grow cluster provisioning, IAM reconciliation, bucket creation, or network configuration into this client. Versioned examples and acceptance jobs exploit the existing submission surface while leaving infrastructure lifecycle with the user's established Google Cloud tooling. They also avoid implying that this project can certify every private-network or organization-policy configuration.

docs.title: 15.1 · Publish one tested AKS workload-identity-to-ADLS reference job
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Identity boundaries are documented; AKS/ADLS and Key Vault rotation require an Azure subscription and credential-rotation fixture.

Required evidence before implementation: On a prepared AKS namespace, the documented SDK/CLI job writes and rereads a known partitioned dataset using at least two executor pods, without account keys or client secrets. A deliberately incorrect application service account fails the negative test. Capture reproducible setup and cleanup instructions.

docs.title: 15.2 · Add a Key Vault CSI mounted-secret recipe with an explicit rotation contract
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Identity boundaries are documented; AKS/ADLS and Key Vault rotation require an Azure subscription and credential-rotation fixture.

Required evidence before implementation: A prepared AKS test shows both pod roles reading the mounted test value without printing it. After rotation, the documented reread/restart path observes the replacement; missing-provider and denied-access cases fail with actionable evidence. Submission plans and logs contain no secret values.

Feedback: Make the identity boundary visible before Azure users edit Helm values. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid turning the project into an Azure resource and credential manager. Creating cloud identities, role assignments, Key Vault synchronization, and networking would duplicate platform tooling and greatly expand the trust boundary. Start with maintained examples and explicit prerequisites; keep production Azure lifecycle ownership with the platform team. Build more only after concrete integration failures justify it.

docs.title: 16.1 · Publish and verify an arbitrary-UID API deployment recipe
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Namespace-scoped deployment guidance is delivered. Arbitrary-UID and disconnected promotion need actual OpenShift admission and registry environments.

Required evidence before implementation: The documented API profile starts with two different non-root UIDs, serves health and readiness, and records a run on a suitably provisioned claim without permission errors; the verification requires no privileged pod or elevated SCC.

docs.title: 16.2 · Provide a disconnected promotion recipe for one complete starter
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Namespace-scoped deployment guidance is delivered. Arbitrary-UID and disconnected promotion need actual OpenShift admission and registry environments.

Required evidence before implementation: A second operator follows the recipe in a namespace whose egress permits only the private registry and required cluster services, starts the API, and completes the lakehouse starter with the recorded image digests and no public artifact requests.

Feedback: Make namespace-scoped installation the first restricted-cluster example. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Do not solve admission friction by granting anyuid or privileged access. Such a shortcut defeats the target operator’s deployment constraints and hides image or volume assumptions. Prefer narrowly documented runtime permissions and verified writable paths; keep administrator policy changes outside this library.

docs.title: 17.1 · A resource-budgeted laptop first-run path
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. First-run routes use existing tested computation. A new laptop installer or automatic failure lab would create platform ownership beyond the client.

Required evidence before implementation: On the documented clean local cluster configuration, a reviewer completes the guide with one driver and one executor, observes the expected result, and reruns it after cleanup without editing source files. A small newcomer trial targets completion within 30 minutes after prerequisites and image downloads are ready.

docs.title: 17.2 · A guided image-failure and recovery lesson
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. First-run routes use existing tested computation. A new laptop installer or automatic failure lab would create platform ownership beyond the client.

Required evidence before implementation: A learner can identify the missing-image condition from evidence, explain why doctor success does not certify image availability, recover without rebuilding the package, and independently identify which pod runs application code.

Feedback: Make scoped permissions the first teaching example. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid a bundled laptop platform installer. Automatically installing Kubernetes, Airflow, the API, storage and a registry would create a large support surface and consume the learner's limited resources. A core-client lab using ordinary existing tools makes each component understandable and keeps the optional integrations optional.

docs.title: 18.1 · Preserve a small, exportable cost-attribution record
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. The resource budget slice is delivered. Cost attribution policy still requires agreement on retained labels, privacy and an external cost system.

Required evidence before implementation: Record two teams sharing a namespace, delete their driver pods, and export every retained run with the correct attribution and unique deployment/run identity; a missing-label fixture must remain explicitly unattributed. Disallowed labels must never enter storage or output.

docs.title: 18.2 · Add an offline resource-envelope budget check
docs.text:
Partially implemented. CPU/memory request envelope and explicit budget checks reject unknown or excessive maxima. Implementation or contract.

Feedback: Keep operational observation times out of spend and utilization claims. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid building a cloud-pricing and chargeback platform. Cloud discounts, shared-node allocation, storage, network charges and billing corrections exceed the recorder's evidence and would create substantial maintenance. Prioritize stable attribution joins and transparent resource envelopes; let an existing organizational cost system compute money and allocations. Do not automatically terminate jobs based on these estimates.

docs.title: 19.1 · Expose an aggregate workload capacity envelope in offline plans
docs.text: Implemented. One shared conservative capacity summary; not a scheduler feasibility guarantee. Implementation or contract.

docs.title: 19.2 · Add a paired driver/executor scheduling audit for existing profiles
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Capacity requests are summarized. Scheduling audits cannot establish quota, placement or autoscaler feasibility offline.

Required evidence before implementation: An intentionally mismatched driver/executor scheduler fails an explicit parity assertion; a documented higher-priority driver passes an allowed difference; an inaccessible executor template remains unknown. Existing jobs without assertions continue to submit unchanged.

Feedback: Describe remote admission limits as per-job bounds, not shared capacity control. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid building an internal fair-share or gang scheduler. An embedded queue introduces durable state, cancellation, resource reservation, fairness, and multi-instance coordination obligations. Prefer transparent capacity summaries and verified integration contracts with an existing scheduler; neither the current shared operator token nor metadata history should become an implicit scheduler database.

docs.title: 20.1 · Publish a repeatable deployment recipe for separate trust boundaries
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Separate trust-boundary deployment guidance is explicit. Per-application identity binding is not sufficient to claim route-wide tenant isolation.

Required evidence before implementation: In the two-department fixture, each credential can submit and inspect its own job; every tested cross-department read or management operation fails without returning workload data. Rendered manifests contain no wildcard ClusterRoleBinding for either API. A documented onboarding exercise requires only substituting department names and existing gateway/secret references.

docs.title: 20.2 · Bind approved applications to their permitted workload identities
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Separate trust-boundary deployment guidance is explicit. Per-application identity binding is not sufficient to claim route-wide tenant isolation.

Required evidence before implementation: A matrix with two applications and two workload identities admits exactly the two intended pairings and rejects both swapped pairings for plan and submit. Rejection occurs before any Kubernetes write. Legacy-policy conversion preserves its original four combinations and clearly identifies that behavior.

Feedback: Keep the operator boundary visible beside namespace allowlists. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid labeling a token-per-team extension as tenant isolation. Multiple tokens alone would leave the shared backend credentials and management surfaces unchanged. Prefer the supported deployment boundary until principal-aware authorization, workload identities and cross-boundary access tests exist throughout the API.

docs.title: 21.1 · Preserve verified gateway actor identity in submission audit events
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Authorization matrix and gateway boundary are documented. Actor audit and renewable credentials need verified gateway identity/expiry contracts.

Required evidence before implementation: A gateway fixture produces attributable allow and deny events that correlate to returned request IDs and accepted run receipts. Forged headers, invalid signatures, wrong audiences and expired assertions cannot obtain attributed execution when the adapter is enabled. Existing shared-token mode remains explicitly unattributed.

docs.title: 21.2 · Add a renewable credential provider to the remote SDK
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Authorization matrix and gateway boundary are documented. Actor audit and renewable credentials need verified gateway identity/expiry contracts.

Required evidence before implementation: One client instance uses token A, then token B after a provider/file update. Expired or malformed credentials cause zero network requests. A submission receiving 401 or losing its response is sent exactly once, and neither logs nor exception messages expose either token.

Feedback: Publish one explicit authorization matrix across deployment modes. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid implementing an identity provider inside spark-on-k8s. User directories, password recovery, session management and provider-specific group synchronization would create a permanent security maintenance burden. Prefer a narrow gateway contract and established identity infrastructure; do not advertise tenant isolation merely because a verified subject becomes available.

docs.title: 22.1 · Strip proxy credentials independently of remote submission mode
docs.text: Implemented. Proxy credential allowlist applies independently of remote-submission mode. Implementation or contract.

docs.title: 22.2 · Define and enforce browser origins for log WebSockets
docs.text:
Implemented. Browser origins checked before log collection; explicit external-origin configuration and non-browser semantics documented. Implementation or contract.

Feedback: Publish the security boundary alongside the reporting policy. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Do not put the operator bearer in browser storage or socket URLs. Solving browser authentication by embedding the shared token in bootstrap data, localStorage, or query strings would expose a powerful reusable credential to more browser code and logs. Preserve the gateway-mediated design and improve its explicit origin and header contracts instead. This does not require expanding the project into an identity platform.

docs.title: 23.1 · Build release containers from a frozen API dependency set
docs.text: Implemented. Container consumes the release wheel and hash-checked frozen API dependencies using a pinned base. Implementation or contract.

docs.title: 23.2 · Publish an artifact inventory that includes the bundled frontend
docs.text:
Implemented bounded scope. Release manifest records package/dependency inputs and hashes; OCI image build requests provenance/SBOM. This is not a vulnerability dashboard. Implementation or contract.

Feedback: Make the release-to-tested-commit relationship explicit. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Avoid an all-purpose security dashboard or blanket vulnerability gate. Start with verifiable release inputs and usable artifact evidence. A custom dashboard adds maintenance, while blocking every advisory across all optional and build dependencies can make releases unpredictable without establishing actual exposure. Define ownership, affected install profiles, and exception handling before adopting a broader gate.

docs.title: 24.1 · Attach policy provenance to submission decision receipts
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Reproducible inputs and metadata limitations are documented. Compliance receipts/exports require a consumer schema, retention policy and trusted actor source.

Required evidence before implementation: An accepted request, denied request, and simulated partial Kubernetes failure each produce correlatable response/event records. Changing the loaded policy changes its digest; formatting-only changes do not. Sentinel secrets never appear in events. Shared-token requests cannot acquire a claimed human identity from client headers.

docs.title: 24.2 · Export a bounded run-evidence snapshot with an explicit coverage manifest
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Reproducible inputs and metadata limitations are documented. Compliance receipts/exports require a consumer schema, retention policy and trusted actor source.

Required evidence before implementation: Concurrent collector updates and pruning during export cannot yield a mixed snapshot. The manifest count matches the artifact; the checksum verifies; namespace filtering remains enforced. Oversized exports return an explicit error. Reviewers can identify collection freshness and retention limitations from the artifact alone.

Feedback: Provide a reproducible operator-deployment example. The clarified behavior and ownership boundaries are captured in the linked implementation or canonical guide; existing support limits remain explicit. Response.

Scope caution accepted: Do not market operational history as a compliance audit trail. Polling misses runs, retention removes records, and shared operator authorization does not identify individual users. Preserve the documented limitations and integrate with external identity and evidence retention systems when needed; avoid unsupported legal compliance claims or a large embedded governance suite.

docs.title: 25.1 · Add an explicit, minimized log-sharing export
docs.text: Implemented. Local bounded excerpt preparation with explicit copy/download scope and stable reading view; no extra server retention. Implementation or contract.

docs.title: 25.2 · Offer a minimal history metadata profile before persistence
docs.text:
Not adopted in this change. Log minimization is delivered. A separate minimal-history profile needs a documented consumer impact and migration story.
