Variable Meaning Default SPARK_ON_K8S_AIRFLOW_SERVICE_URL Administrator-configured Spark API base URL reachable from the Airflow API server. Required to register the tab. unset; tab disabled SPARK_ON_K8S_AIRFLOW_PUBLIC_URL Browser-reachable base URL for external Spark UI and history links. service URL SPARK_ON_K8S_AIRFLOW_ALLOW_WRITES Set to true to permit kill/delete requests after task ownership and Airflow permissions are checked. false

Both URLs may include a deployment path prefix and must be HTTP(S) URLs without embedded credentials, query parameters or fragments. The service URL is chosen by the administrator, not by browser input. The plugin does not forward the browser's Airflow credentials to that service. Keep the Spark API behind appropriate network access controls; Airflow authentication does not protect a separately exposed Spark API or its external links.

If spark_on_k8s_service_url is set on an operator, it must match the configured service or public URL. Use the public URL to keep the existing Spark Job UI link browser-accessible. Set ui_reverse_proxy=True on the operator to offer the live Spark UI link. Airflow deployments under a URL prefix are supported; no root-relative plugin URL needs to be configured.

The tab uses the selected DAG, run, task, mapped index or region, and current attempt to resolve a small metadata record in XCom. Live data is checked against the spark-on-k8s.io/airflow-task annotation written on the driver by the operator. A mismatched or missing ownership annotation is rejected. A retry may adopt its own earlier attempt's driver; another task's driver cannot be selected by editing XCom. Older task submissions without the new metadata retain their existing operator links but cannot use the task tab's live features.

Read requests require Airflow access to the task; log streaming additionally requires task-log access. Kill and delete also require the corresponding Airflow write permission and SPARK_ON_K8S_AIRFLOW_ALLOW_WRITES=true. Log connections and write requests must come from the Airflow page's origin. The Spark API's own permissions still apply.

After the driver pod is deleted, the tab shows only the saved task-local application ID with unknown status. It offers an external history link only when the Spark API reports a configured History Server. It disables live logs and actions, and does not fetch history records using XCom alone. The external history link requires the event logging and History Server setup described above. While a driver exists and ownership is verified, the tab can fetch that application's history metadata through the configured Spark API.

The native tab checks the Spark API configuration before enabling history. An unconfigured History Server does not produce a warning; a configured server that cannot be reached still does. Older API services without the capability endpoint retain live application features but omit optional history links until upgraded.

The native task log proxy accepts individual text messages up to 16 MiB, including long driver log lines. A larger message interrupts the stream rather than being silently truncated. The proxy uses a small receive queue to keep buffering bounded; the console's separate line-count limit still applies.

docs.title: Automation and run identities
docs.text: These features describe the current source. For shell scripts and CI, use --output json instead of parsing human-readable progress messages.

docs.title: Submit and observe a run
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s app submit \
  --namespace spark \
  --image registry.example.com/team/job:version \
  --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py \
  --name daily-report \
  --wait --timeout 900 --output json > result.json

The command writes one JSON document to stdout. Progress and driver logs go to stderr in JSON mode, so --logs --output json > result.json 2> driver.log keeps both streams separate. --logs waits for a terminal application state after the log stream ends; end-of-stream alone does not prove that a job succeeded.

A successful waiting submission has this shape:

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "operation": "submit",
  "namespace": "spark",
  "error": null,
  "run": {
    "namespace": "spark",
    "app_id": "daily-report-20261107120000",
    "driver_pod": "daily-report-20261107120000-driver",
    "driver_uid": "5bdceeb0-7fa8-4f72-823b-80f26e6195c4"
  },
  "status": "Succeeded"
}

Without --wait or --logs, exit code 0 means the application resources were submitted, and status is null. It does not mean the workload succeeded. The receipt identifies the actual generated application ID and driver pod. It is retained in runtime error output if submission succeeded before waiting failed, timed out, or was interrupted. An error during resource creation can leave partial resources. The client records a confirmed driver UID immediately after receiving its creation response. Results include submission_phase (preparing, creating_resources, driver_created, resources_created) so a later owner-reference or Service failure can still return the known driver identity. If creation itself has an ambiguous transport result, no confirmed receipt is invented. Inspect the cluster before retrying.

--timeout takes positive, finite seconds and requires a wait or log waiter on submission. It limits observation after submission, including a running job and a quiet log stream. It does not bound initial resource creation or an external Kubernetes credential plugin. The default is unlimited observation. The existing SPARK_ON_K8S_STARTUP_TIMEOUT remains a separate limit for a pending driver. Neither timeout nor interruption automatically kills or deletes the application.

To observe a previously submitted application:

spark-on-k8s app wait --namespace spark --app-id "$APP_ID" \
  --timeout 900 --output json
spark-on-k8s app status --namespace spark --app-id "$APP_ID" --output json
spark-on-k8s apps list --namespace spark --output json

A status or wait document contains schema_version, operation, namespace, app_id, status, and error. A list document contains the same common fields plus items, an array of { "app_id": "...", "namespace": "..." } objects; it does not contain app_id or status at the top level. On a list error, items is null. Listing does not make a status request for each application.

Runtime errors use error: { "code": "...", "message": "..." } with codes api_error, operation_error, not_found, timeout, or interrupted. JSON error messages exclude Kubernetes response bodies. Receipts do not contain submitted configuration or secrets. Driver logs remain application-controlled data and may contain sensitive information. Consumers should check schema_version, tolerate additional fields, and avoid depending on object-key order or human messages. CLI argument errors are reported by Click on stderr before execution and do not produce a JSON document. --help remains human-readable.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Submission accepted, successful query, or waiting workload succeeded 1 Operation, configuration, or Kubernetes API failure 2 Invalid CLI arguments or options 3 Waiting workload ended in Failed 4 Requested application or Kubernetes resource was not found 5 Observation, startup, or transport timeout 6 Waiting workload outcome is unknown; success was not established 130 User interruption

Workload outcome codes apply to app wait and app submit --wait / --logs. app status returns 0 when the query succeeds, even if the reported status is Failed. app logs remains a standalone streaming command; follow it with app wait when a script needs the workload result.

Shells configured with set -e stop on a failed workload. To retain and inspect failure output, explicitly capture the exit code:

exit_code=0
spark-on-k8s app wait -n spark --app-id "$APP_ID" --output json \
  > result.json || exit_code=$?
cat result.json
exit "$exit_code"

docs.title: Python run handles
docs.text:
Existing callers can continue using submit_app(...), which returns the driver pod name as a string. submit_run(...) accepts the same arguments and returns an immutable RunHandle with namespace, app_id, and driver_pod fields:

from spark_on_k8s.client import SparkOnK8S

client = SparkOnK8S()
run = client.submit_run(
    namespace="spark",
    image="registry.example.com/team/job:version",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
    app_name="daily-report",
    app_waiter="no_wait",
)
print(run.to_dict())
client.app_manager.wait_for_app(
    namespace=run.namespace, pod_name=run.driver_pod, timeout=900,
)
status = client.app_manager.app_status(
    namespace=run.namespace, pod_name=run.driver_pod,
)

Python callers explicitly inspect the final status; the SDK does not convert it into a process exit code. Both submission methods update last_submitted_run and the existing last_submitted_app_id. A later attempt clears these properties before validation, so a failed submission cannot return a previous run's identity. Keep the returned handle when submitting multiple runs with one client. These per-client convenience properties are not intended for concurrent submissions.

For SDK submission with app_waiter="wait" or "log", the optional wait_timeout sets an observation budget after resource creation. Managers also accept timeout on wait_for_app and stream_logs; expiration raises TimeoutError. submit_run does not support dry runs. A handle contains no credentials, clients, or automatic reattachment behavior.

docs.title: Save identity before waiting
docs.text:
Add --receipt-file run.json to app submit, job submit, or sql submit. The parent directory must exist and the destination must be new. A private file (mode 0600) is published atomically after submission, before log streaming or waiting. A timeout, interruption, or observer crash does not remove it. Existing receipts are never overwritten. Stdout still contains a single final result.

spark-on-k8s job submit job.yaml --profile production \
  --receipt-file run.json --output json > result.json

The file contains schema_version: 1 and run with namespace, application ID, driver name and Kubernetes UID. Use its namespace and application ID with app wait to resume observation from another process using the same cluster. Receipts contain no credentials, kubeconfig or cluster endpoint. Select the correct cluster explicitly; a receipt is an identity, not authorization.

A known driver receipt is also saved when a later resource-creation step fails. If receipt persistence fails too, the original submission failure remains primary and receipt_error describes the storage failure. A receipt cannot recover an unknown submission response or make data writes idempotent. If local publication fails after submission, the command fails and its final JSON still contains the known run. Investigate that run before retrying.

docs.title: Cancel the recorded run
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s app cancel --receipt run.json --output json

Cancellation reads the current pod, verifies its UID, application label and driver role, then sends a Kubernetes UID precondition with the deletion request. A stale receipt cannot delete a replacement pod with the same name. Older receipts without a UID cannot use this command. accepted: true means the API accepted deletion; it does not establish that executors, volumes or finalizers have finished cleanup. --force requests zero grace period and still preserves the identity checks. No timeout automatically invokes cancellation.

docs.title: Contract coverage and lifecycle ownership
docs.text:
Command family Structured success Structured runtime failures Completion meaning app submit/wait, job submit, sql submit --output json Versioned result after CLI parsing Inspect terminal status; detached submit means accepted app status, apps list, app cancel --output json Versioned result Query/deletion request succeeded, not data correctness job validate --output json, per-profile results Validation failures in result Offline validation only job plan --output json Load/build errors remain Click text Redacted preview, no reservation connect check --output json Bounded check result Tiny query succeeded on existing server legacy kill/delete/log commands Text Text Signal/deletion request or log observation

CLI usage errors still follow Click's text/exit-code contract. Do not assume every JSON-capable command serializes every failure.

SparkJob is loaded by a client; it is not a Kubernetes custom resource or a reconciled controller. The caller submits and decides whether to observe or retry. Kubernetes runs the created workload after the client exits. Airflow owns scheduling and task retry policy when its operator is used. SDK/CLI observation timeouts retain the application; Airflow startup timeouts deliberately delete it. A kill signal is a termination request, not evidence of a completed streaming drain or checkpoint.

Disable caching for workflow submission steps. Reusing a cached receipt does not establish that this workflow executed the data job. Observe the same run before starting downstream consumers; retrying observation and resubmitting are different actions. Use one active submission per SparkOnK8S instance: the compatibility last_submitted_* attributes are mutable and shared-instance concurrent submission is not supported. Persist the returned immutable run handle per operation.

docs.title: Chart deployment boundaries
docs.text: These controls describe the current source chart. Published charts, API images and Python packages have independent release histories; inspect the selected chart and image before upgrading. The chart is an API/console deployment with an optional Spark History Server. It does not deploy a Spark scheduler, create a cloud workload identity, or configure applications submitted through the SDK.

docs.title: Select the image explicitly
docs.text:
The API image uses image.digest when set. Otherwise it uses image.tag; an explicitly empty tag opts into that chart's appVersion fallback. A version tag is clearer than latest, but only a verified digest fixes the image contents.

The source chart requires an explicit compatible image tag or digest while its appVersion is unreleased. Release packaging sets a qualified application version, which becomes the default image tag. Building or rendering the local chart does not build an API image.

The optional History Server has a separate image lifecycle. Enabling sparkHistory.enabled requires an explicit sparkHistory.image.tag or sparkHistory.image.digest; there is no implicit API-version or latest fallback. For both images, a digest takes precedence over a simultaneously set tag. Use repository without an embedded tag or digest, and put the complete sha256: plus 64 hexadecimal characters in digest.

No History Server image version is qualified by these chart-rendering checks. Validate your selected History image, event-log storage and Spark runtime together before deployment. An explicitly selected latest tag remains accepted for intentional development use; it does not make the deployment reproducible.

docs.title: Start with scoped, externally managed access
docs.text:
The source includes chart/examples/production-values.yaml. It uses explicit analytics,batch namespaces, the preprovisioned spark-observer service account, external RBAC, a ClusterIP service, and illustrative resource reservations. Its REQUIRED_SHA256_DIGEST placeholder deliberately fails validation. Set a digest you have verified for the selected API image repository:

# Set API_IMAGE_DIGEST to the verified sha256:... digest; no sample image is implied.
: "${API_IMAGE_DIGEST:?Set the verified API image digest}"
helm lint ./chart -f chart/examples/production-values.yaml \
  --set-string image.digest="$API_IMAGE_DIGEST"
helm template spark-console ./chart --namespace spark-system \
  -f chart/examples/production-values.yaml \
  --set-string image.digest="$API_IMAGE_DIGEST" > rendered-console.yaml

Provision the release namespace and named service account before installation. The administrator must grant that account the needed access in the selected application namespaces. Review the rendered resources and adjust the example's namespaces, resource requests and limits for your deployment. The example does not establish availability, throughput or cloud-identity compatibility.

The default readOnly: true remains unchanged. With chart-managed RBAC and an explicit namespace string, the chart creates namespace Roles and RoleBindings. namespaces: "*" intentionally selects a cluster-wide binding instead. Neither namespace selection nor hiding UI buttons provides user or tenant authorization; use the remote-submission security boundary.

docs.title: Decide who owns the account and permissions
docs.text:
rbac.create controls API roles and bindings independently of serviceAccount.create. Its default, null, follows serviceAccount.create to preserve existing rendering. The History Server has its own service-account setting; API RBAC settings do not grant History Server storage permissions.

API configuration Account created by Helm Roles/bindings created by Helm serviceAccount.create: true, rbac.create: null Yes Yes; legacy default serviceAccount.create: false, rbac.create: null No No; legacy external-account behavior serviceAccount.create: false, explicit serviceAccount.name, rbac.create: true No Yes, bound to that account in the release namespace serviceAccount.create: true, rbac.create: false Yes No serviceAccount.create: false, rbac.create: false No No; fully external ownership

The chart requires an explicit account name when creating RBAC for an external account. readOnly only changes chart-managed permissions; it cannot reduce permissions already granted externally. The namespace edit Role supports existing management actions, but it is not a complete grant for every optional submission resource. Review the actual templates and grant any required Secret/ConfigMap operations deliberately for a remote-submission deployment.

When changing ownership on an installed release, inspect the Helm diff first. Setting a create flag to false removes previously managed resources from the release; Helm can delete them during upgrade. Arrange the replacement permissions and deliberate resource-ownership transfer before that upgrade. Do not assume that changing the flag alone preserves the existing account or grants.

docs.title: Keep the four workload identities separate
docs.text:
Role Identity and metadata inputs Image and image-pull inputs API/console Chart serviceAccount.*, podLabels, podAnnotations; its Kubernetes credentials observe/manage applications Chart image.*, imagePullSecrets Spark driver Submission namespace, service_account, driver_labels, driver_annotations and driver template Submission image, image_pull_policy; driver template for supported pull-secret customization Spark executors Application executor template and Spark configuration for the chosen runtime; executor_labels and executor_annotations Application image/configuration and executor template; API chart pull secrets are not inherited History Server Chart sparkHistory.serviceAccount.*, sparkHistory.podLabels, sparkHistory.podAnnotations; independent event-storage identity sparkHistory.image.*; chart imagePullSecrets is applied to its pod too

These roles may share an account when that is intentional; they do not need to. The resolved submission service_account overrides a service account written inside the driver template. API chart account annotations and labels do not become application defaults. See driver templates for the supported merge rules and inspect the generated driver plan.

Cloud IAM bindings, storage credentials and admission policies remain owned by the cluster administrator. A successful doctor check establishes only its reported caller checks and account existence; it does not prove that a driver, executor or History Server can access your object store. Cloud-specific recipes and arbitrary-user container support are not qualified by this chart validation suite.

docs.title: Understand the scaling controls
docs.text:
Control What it scales Owner Chart replicaCount or autoscaling.* API/console replicas API deployment owner Application ExecutorInstances / Spark dynamic allocation Executors within one Spark application Application owner Kubernetes cluster/node-pool autoscaler Available worker nodes Cluster/cloud administrator

Increasing autoscaling.maxReplicas does not increase an application's executor ceiling or create nodes. The optional History Server has its own sparkHistory.replicaCount and autoscaling settings. CPU/memory HPA targets need appropriate container requests and the cluster's metrics support; setting a target to null or 0 disables that metric, and an enabled HPA requires at least one positive target.

The metadata recorder is separate from the Spark History Server. Enabling runHistory requires exactly one API replica, no API autoscaling, an existing writable persistent claim, and one to twenty explicit namespace entries. The chart uses a Recreate rollout. It neither provisions the claim nor validates its filesystem locking behavior; use supported block/local storage, rehearse backups and allow for rollout downtime.

docs.title: Validate before installation
docs.text:
values.schema.json checks chart-owned types, image references, service ports, namespace forms, HPA bounds and recorder settings. Template guards cover cross-field comparisons and reserved volume names. Run both helm lint and helm template: lint can suppress template-level fail messages, while rendering rejects those cross-field conflicts. namespaces remains a comma-separated string; runHistory.namespaces is a YAML list. Kubernetes passthrough objects, such as affinity, resources and security contexts, remain open so normal cluster-specific fields are accepted.

Rendering checks do not validate cloud permissions, image availability, storage access or API server admission. Raw env overrides still take precedence over chart-generated environment settings and remain the operator's responsibility. An ingress.tls entry terminates TLS before the API, so browser log streams are rejected until env sets SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WEBSOCKET_ALLOWED_ORIGINS to the public https:// origins; see browser origins. Use the development guide for the Helm regression suite and release guidance for the artifact publication boundary.

docs.title: Preparing the next chart release
docs.text:
The source chart marks appVersion as unreleased and requires an explicit compatible image.tag or image.digest. The release publisher sets the package's qualified application version; an empty image tag then selects that version. API 0.12.1 does not implement /ready and is not compatible with these probes. Do not publish this chart against that older API image. The helm-release workflow refuses an app_version below 0.13.0 or without a published ghcr.io/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s image, and a chart_version that the chart repository already lists. Run it only after the package release has published the API image, selecting that release tag in the workflow's ref selector so the chart source matches the qualified application.

When upgrading a release installed from published chart 0.3.0, pass your values file again, or use --reset-then-reuse-values (Helm 3.14 and later), instead of --reuse-values. --reuse-values replaces this chart's defaults with the old release's values, including its latest image tags, and omits new settings such as rbac, runHistory and metrics. The chart schema rejects such an upgrade with a missing properties error before rendering.

Shared RBAC resource names now include the release namespace identity. Existing installations can set rbac.legacyNames: true to retain their old names during an upgrade. New installations should use the default false, allowing identical release names in separate namespaces. To migrate existing installations, render and review both RBAC sets, ensure the new bindings exist before removing old bindings, and verify access under the service account. Switching the value in a normal Helm upgrade replaces the old resources; schedule that transition if a brief permissions interruption is unacceptable. Never reuse legacy names for two releases managing the same shared scope.

History configuration updates now roll its Deployment automatically. History affinity and tolerations are passed to the Pod. The rare long-name suffix collision is disambiguated; existing installations using those colliding names need a reviewed recreation because Deployment selectors are immutable.

docs.title: Experimental managed dbt
docs.text:
Run a dbt Core command against temporary Spark compute on an existing Kubernetes cluster. The wrapper creates one server when dbt first opens a connection, shares it across dbt worker threads, and deletes its driver, executors and private Services when the command ends. Choose Thrift or Spark Connect in the profile; you do not create the server yourself.

Experimental, separately installed integration

This feature lives in integrations/dbt and is not part of a normal spark-on-k8s installation. Its profile and Python interfaces may change. The initial compatibility target is dbt Core 1.12.6, dbt-spark 1.11.0, Spark/client 4.3.0, PyHive 0.7.0, and Thrift 0.25.0. It is a Python dbt Core adapter, not a dbt Fusion, dbt Cloud or dbt v2 integration. SQL models, seeds and data tests are supported; Python models are explicitly rejected. dbt clone is explicitly rejected in this experiment.

docs.title: Prepare the platform
docs.text:
The platform owner supplies:

  • An existing namespace and driver service account with the permissions described in server setup. This integration does not create or delete the Kubernetes cluster, namespace or RBAC.
  • A compatible Spark image with the bundled Connect or HiveThriftServer2 JAR.
  • A shared warehouse reachable by the driver and executors and an external Hive metastore reachable by each new driver. The profile requires both. An embedded driver-local metastore would disappear when the driver is deleted. Driver-local warehouse paths, including file://, are rejected because this experiment does not mount persistent driver volumes. Supply a remote filesystem URI and its Spark connector; the integration fixture tests HDFS.
  • A trusted network for the private, plaintext server and catalog endpoints. The experiment uses Thrift auth: NONE; it is not a multi-tenant gateway.

For a local client, install kubectl and provide an explicit kubeconfig path and context. The wrapper opens a loopback-only tunnel to its driver, using an OS-assigned local port. For a client already inside Kubernetes, set in_cluster: true and omit both kubeconfig fields; it connects to the private Service directly. The client's identity needs permission to create/read/delete its driver and Services, read the namespace/service account and observe executor pods, Services and ConfigMaps (including list permission for garbage-collection checks); local access also needs pod port-forward permission.

docs.title: Install from the repository
docs.text:
Until the experimental distribution is separately published, build both wheels from the same checkout. These commands use an isolated Python 3.12 environment:

# From the spark-on-k8s repository root:
uv build --wheel --out-dir dist/dbt-experiment
uv build --project integrations/dbt --wheel --out-dir dist/dbt-experiment
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv-dbt
uv pip install --python .venv-dbt/bin/python dist/dbt-experiment/*.whl
uv pip check --python .venv-dbt/bin/python

For reproducible development/testing, use the separate lockfile instead:

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT="$PWD/.venv-dbt" uv sync \
  --project integrations/dbt --locked --python 3.12 --group test

The integration declares PyHive and patched Thrift directly instead of selecting dbt-spark[pyhive], whose current extra caps Thrift below the patched releases. Do not add that extra to this environment: let the normal dependency resolver keep the transport compatible. Thrift's protocol size/recursion protections remain enabled; unusually large individual result fields can be rejected by those limits.

The package accepts Python 3.11–3.13. Kubernetes execution is tested with Python 3.12. The independent lockfile prevents dbt's dependencies from changing the normal SDK, API or Airflow environments.

docs.title: Configure a managed profile
docs.text:
Use this profile in your dbt project's profiles.yml, replacing the namespace, service account, kubeconfig, metastore and warehouse with your platform values:

analytics:
  target: connect
  outputs:
    connect:
      type: spark_on_k8s
      method: connect
      schema: analytics
      threads: 2
      compute:
        kube_config_file: /absolute/path/to/kubeconfig
        kube_context: my-context
        namespace: spark
        service_account: spark
        image: apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu
        server_jar: local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar
        startup_timeout: 180
        cleanup_timeout: 120
        driver_resources: {cpu: 1, memory: 1024, memory_overhead: 512}
        executor_resources: {cpu: 1, memory: 1024, memory_overhead: 512}
        executor_instances: {initial: 2}
        spark_conf:
          spark.sql.catalogImplementation: hive
          spark.sql.warehouse.dir: hdfs://namenode.data.svc:8020/warehouse
          spark.hadoop.hive.metastore.uris: thrift://metastore.data.svc:9083
          spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: '4'

Your dbt_project.yml must select profile: analytics. To use Thrift, change target and the output name to thrift, set method: thrift, and replace server_jar with:

server_jar: local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-hive-thriftserver_2.13-4.3.0.jar

The adapter selects the host and port. Do not supply host, port, SPARK_REMOTE or the upstream method: session workaround. Connect uses a separate explicit remote session for each dbt connection. Thrift uses PyHive's HiveServer2 protocol, not a JDBC client.

compute accepts the explicit image, namespace, service account, resource, executor-allocation, package and node-selector fields of ConnectServerConfig, plus the cluster-selection fields above, startup_timeout, cleanup_timeout and poll_interval (positive seconds, at most 3600). Thrift fixes its managed port to 10000. Managed identity, ports and routing cannot be overridden through spark_conf. Put static Hive/catalog configuration in compute.spark_conf; server_side_parameters accepts runtime spark.sql.* settings; catalog, warehouse, Hive metastore and extension settings are excluded.

docs.title: Run dbt with automatic compute cleanup
docs.text:
Use the installed executable's absolute path if your current directory is a separate dbt project:

/path/to/spark-on-k8s/.venv-dbt/bin/spark-on-k8s-dbt run -- \
  build --project-dir /path/to/analytics --profiles-dir /path/to/analytics

Every command is an independent invocation. For example, seed, build, run-operation, test and docs generate can each use the same wrapper:

/path/to/spark-on-k8s/.venv-dbt/bin/spark-on-k8s-dbt run -- \
  docs generate --project-dir /path/to/analytics --profiles-dir /path/to/analytics

The server survives dbt's intermediate connection cleanup, including the compilation phase of docs generate. It is removed only when the entire command finishes. Tables remain in the external warehouse/catalog for the next invocation. Commands that never open a database connection do not provision compute. Using plain dbt with this managed adapter reports that the wrapper is required; there is no unbounded background server hidden behind a connection-close hook.

Statements are not automatically replayed (query_retries must be 0). Spark SQL is not transactional: failure and cancellation can leave successfully written tables or rows. Review dbt's normal incremental/idempotency behavior before retrying. Connect supports cancellation but does not accept query_timeout in this initial version; Thrift retains dbt-spark's query timeout setting. Thrift serializes requests on each connection and limits acquisition of the request lock and individual blocking socket operations to 15 seconds. These transport limits do not cap the full SQL execution time: queries run asynchronously and the adapter polls for completion. A failed transport is closed rather than reused, and statements are not replayed. Connect buffers SQL results for dbt metadata/seed/materialization operations; it is not a streaming query-results interface.

docs.title: Receipts, failure and recovery
docs.text:
The wrapper prints the recovery receipt path to stderr. By default each invocation gets a unique directory under .spark-on-k8s/dbt/ in the working directory. Set --receipt-dir /new/private/directory before -- to choose it explicitly; the directory must not already exist. Receipts have private file permissions and retain resource UIDs and cluster selection, not the original Spark configuration or its catalog credentials. Protect the dbt profile and normal dbt logs separately.

Normal success, dbt failures and a graceful Ctrl-C/SIGTERM all attempt cleanup. Exit codes are 0 for success, 1 for a dbt execution failure, 2 for invocation or cleanup errors, and 130/143 for interruption. A cleanup failure preserves an already failing dbt exit code and records the separate cleanup failure. A successful command becomes nonzero if cleanup fails. Cleanup verifies the recorded namespace, driver and Service identities and observes disappearance before reporting success. It never deletes the warehouse or metastore.

A hard kill, machine loss, unavailable Kubernetes API, or ambiguous creation can leave compute running. After inspecting a complete receipt, retry safe cleanup:

/path/to/spark-on-k8s/.venv-dbt/bin/spark-on-k8s-dbt cleanup \
  --receipt /path/to/invocation/receipt.json

Deletion refuses changed identities and incomplete receipts. In those cases, inspect the recorded application and Kubernetes UIDs manually; do not delete by name alone or discard the receipt. No external orphan-reaper controller is installed. Avoid concurrent invocations targeting the same dbt output tables; separate process ownership protects compute, not conflicting SQL writes.

docs.title: What the tests exercise
docs.text: The integration harness runs installed wheels on disposable Kubernetes with a shared HDFS warehouse and an external metastore fixture. It checks both transports, parallel dbt workers, seeds/models/data tests, fresh compute across commands, catalog persistence, documentation generation, failed SQL and graceful cancellation. Fixture storage is temporary and is not a production storage deployment recipe.

docs.title: Diagnose a Spark application
docs.text:
These commands are available from the current source tree. Check the documentation for your installed release before using them with a published package.

Diagnostics collect a bounded snapshot of driver and executor pod states and Kubernetes events. They explain observed image-pull failures, scheduling constraints, denied operations, OOM kills, crash loops and unavailable persistent volume claims. Each finding contains a stable code, severity, affected resource, evidence and a suggested next step. An unsuccessful exit code alone is not treated as proof of an OOM kill or another specific cause.

docs.title: Inspect an application
docs.text:
Use the application ID returned by submission:

spark-on-k8s app diagnose --namespace spark --app-id YOUR_APPLICATION_ID
spark-on-k8s app diagnose --namespace spark --app-id YOUR_APPLICATION_ID --output json

The SDK accepts either an application ID or an exact driver pod name:

from spark_on_k8s.client import SparkOnK8S

spark = SparkOnK8S()
report = spark.diagnose_app(namespace="spark", app_id="YOUR_APPLICATION_ID")
print(report.to_dict())

# Useful when the driver name was truncated or when inspecting an existing pod.
report = spark.diagnose_app(namespace="spark", pod_name="YOUR_DRIVER_POD")

The JSON report has schema_version: 1, namespace, app_id, driver_pod, findings, inspected_pods, inspected_events and incomplete. A report with no findings means that no specific problem was observed. It does not establish that the application is healthy. Events and previous container termination states may describe earlier attempts that have since recovered.

Collection reads at most 20 executors and 100 events per inspected pod by default. --pod-limit (1–50) and --event-limit (1–200) adjust those limits; the SDK accepts the same parameters and a positive timeout of at most 30 seconds (10 by default). Collection uses one executor page and one event page per inspected pod, without following pagination. A limit, denied read or timeout produces an incomplete report while retaining available evidence. A failed initial driver lookup produces an error.

Executor selection stays within the chosen namespace, uses Spark's application label, and verifies each executor's owner UID against the driver. Events must match the inspected pod UID, so events for a replaced pod with the same name are excluded. No logs, environment values, Secret contents or PVC contents are fetched. Event messages can still contain workload-specific information; share reports with the same care as Kubernetes events.

docs.title: Console and Airflow task tab
docs.text:
Open application Details in the standalone console to see the same findings. The JSON endpoint is:

GET /webserver/api/apps/{namespace}/pods/{driver_pod}/diagnostics

It returns { "application": { ... }, "diagnosis": { ... } }. The two objects come from the same inspected driver pod. Query parameters pod_limit and event_limit use the bounds above. The endpoint permits up to five seconds for the initial driver lookup, followed by the bounded collection budget.

The optional Airflow task tab uses the shared diagnostics panel. Its backend resolves the task's application and checks the driver ownership annotation against the authorized task before returning findings. It does not accept a browser-supplied namespace or application ID. Diagnostics are unavailable after the driver is deleted; the task's history link remains separate. When the Spark API enables remote bearer authentication, the Airflow service URL must use a trusted gateway that authenticates the Airflow backend and injects that credential, or a separate restricted internal API. See remote submission deployment.

The API caller needs namespaced pod reads and list access to core events. Current source chart namespace Roles include this event permission. For an existing installation using an older chart or a custom service account, an administrator must review and add the permission before event collection can succeed. The page can still show pod evidence when event access is denied. API authentication and task authorization continue to apply; diagnostics do not grant additional access.

docs.title: Check cluster prerequisites
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s doctor --namespace spark --service-account spark
spark-on-k8s doctor --namespace spark --service-account spark --output json

doctor reads the named service account and submits non-persistent Kubernetes SelfSubjectAccessReview requests for the authenticated caller's application-management permissions. It does not impersonate the driver or apply resources. Service-account existence and the caller's access do not prove that the driver can create executors: driver_permissions_verified remains false. A denied or unavailable review is reported explicitly.

The caller checks cover pod creation, lookup, listing and deletion; driver log reads; service and ConfigMap creation; and event listing. They are targeted prerequisites, not an exhaustive validation of every optional workload feature. Cluster network reachability from the driver, image contents, admission policies and storage availability still require runtime evidence.

To prepare a namespace-scoped baseline driver role for administrator review, render manifests offline:

spark-on-k8s doctor --namespace spark --service-account spark --emit-rbac > driver-rbac.yaml

This command prints a Role and RoleBinding and never contacts Kubernetes. It does not create the namespace or service account and does not apply the manifests. The binding references the existing service account. The role allows Spark to manage pods, services and ConfigMaps within that namespace; collection deletion is limited to services and ConfigMaps for Spark cleanup. It grants no cluster-wide permissions, Secret access or pod exec access. Optional features such as dynamically created PVCs may need additional permissions that an administrator should review separately.

See the upstream Spark Kubernetes service-account guidance and Kubernetes RBAC guidance when adapting the baseline to your workload.

docs.title: Driver pod templates
docs.text:
The source version supports a Kubernetes Pod template for the driver through the Python client, CLI and both Airflow operators. This feature does not require a Spark operator or a custom resource. Install from source until a release includes it; see installation.

Use a template for settings such as pod/container security contexts, affinity, image pull secrets, sidecars, init containers and additional volumes. The client merges the template into the same driver pod it normally submits.

docs.title: Submit a template
docs.text:
Save this as driver.yaml. The application image still comes from the submission arguments, so the selected container does not need an image in the template.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    team: analytics
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 185
    fsGroup: 185
  containers:
    - name: driver
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        capabilities:
          drop: [ALL]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: scratch
          mountPath: /scratch
  volumes:
    - name: scratch
      emptyDir: {}

Select a user ID supported by your application image and ensure its working directories are writable. A template configures the driver only; use an executor template for executor pod settings.

from spark_on_k8s.client import SparkOnK8S

SparkOnK8S().submit_app(
    image="registry.example.com/team/spark-job:1.0",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    driver_pod_template="./driver.yaml",
    app_waiter="log",
)

spark-on-k8s app submit \
  --image registry.example.com/team/spark-job:1.0 \
  --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py \
  --namespace spark \
  --service-account spark \
  --driver-pod-template ./driver.yaml \
  --logs

driver_pod_template accepts YAML text, a local path string, a pathlib.Path, or a Python mapping. The CLI accepts YAML text or a local path. Files are read on the machine submitting the application; this option does not fetch remote URLs.

docs.title: Select the driver container
docs.text:
A template can contain additional containers. The client selects the container named driver, or the sole container if there is only one. Otherwise, specify driver_container_name="spark-main" or --driver-container-name spark-main. An explicit name must exist. An ambiguous or missing selection is an error.

The selected container becomes the first container in the submitted pod, retaining its name. Other containers keep their relative order and settings. Logs and kill operations target this selected container; the client also sets kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container for interactive kubectl use.

Ordinary sidecars must exit for the pod to finish. A sidecar that keeps running also keeps pod-based waiting and Airflow tasks running. Where supported by your cluster, Kubernetes native sidecars in initContainers with restartPolicy: Always provide a lifecycle that ends with the application containers. Sidecar lifecycle is controlled by Kubernetes, not by this client.

docs.title: Merge rules
docs.text:
The template is the starting point. Submission arguments and their resolved configuration defaults supply the generated fields below. In particular, omitting an argument does not make a template image, service account or CPU/memory setting override the client's configured default. Input mappings are not modified.

Field Result Pod name and namespace Generated application pod name and submission namespace. spark-app-id, spark-app-name, spark-role, spark-ui-proxy labels Managed application identity and proxy settings; template values are discarded. Other labels and annotations Template entries are retained; explicit driver entries override matching keys. Service account and restart policy Submission service account and Never; the deprecated serviceAccount alias is removed. Selected container image, image pull policy and arguments Generated from submission options and Spark configuration. Selected container command Removed, so the application image's Spark entrypoint runs the generated driver arguments. Selected container CPU and memory requests/limits Generated from driver_resources or configured defaults. Other resources, such as ephemeral storage or GPU limits, are retained. Environment variables Merged by name; generated values win, including spark.kubernetes.driverEnv.* properties and the managed SPARK_DRIVER_BIND_ADDRESS. See driver environment variables for precedence and validation. Environment sources (envFrom) Template sources first, then generated secret references; identical entries are not duplicated. Volumes, init containers Merged by name; an explicit matching entry replaces the entire template entry. Driver volume mounts Merged by mount path; an explicit matching entry replaces the entire template entry. Container ports Merged by name, or by port/protocol for unnamed entries; generated driver/UI ports win on matching keys. Node selector Merged by key, with explicit driver selectors winning. Host aliases Merged by IP, with explicit driver aliases winning. Tolerations Template entries followed by explicit driver entries, without exact duplicates. Other pod/container fields Preserved, including security contexts, affinity, image pull secrets and sidecar settings.

Lists with duplicate merge keys are rejected rather than resolved by position. Server-assigned metadata, owner references, generateName, and status are not accepted. Templates cannot supply annotations in the reserved spark-on-k8s.io/ namespace. Keep that namespace available for project-managed ownership metadata; use your own annotation prefix for application metadata.

Loading, container selection and merge validation finish before any Kubernetes Secret, ConfigMap, Pod or Service is created. This is not a complete Kubernetes schema validator: the API server still validates other fields and enforces cluster admission policies. Template settings do not bypass those policies.

docs.title: Airflow
docs.text:
Both SparkOnK8SOperator and SparkSqlOnK8SOperator accept the same template and container-selection arguments. These fields support Airflow templating and DAG serialization on Airflow 2.11 and Airflow 3.

from spark_on_k8s.airflow.operators import SparkOnK8SOperator

application = SparkOnK8SOperator(
    task_id="application",
    image="registry.example.com/team/spark-job:1.0",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    driver_pod_template={
        "apiVersion": "v1",
        "kind": "Pod",
        "metadata": {"labels": {"run-date": "{{ ds }}"}},
        "spec": {"containers": [{"name": "driver"}]},
    },
)

For a file path, Airflow renders the path string, then the SDK reads that file on the worker. File contents are not separately rendered by Airflow. Pass inline YAML or a mapping when the template contents themselves contain Jinja expressions. See the Airflow guide for connection and deployment setup.

docs.title: Application examples
docs.text: These examples describe the current source checkout. Run build and submission commands from the repository root, with namespace spark and service account spark configured as described in Getting Started. The example Dockerfiles default to the Apache Spark 3.5.9 image. To build them with Spark 4, set the image and matching Java dependency versions as described in Spark compatibility. For scheduled jobs, see the Airflow guide.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
In this example, we use a small PySpark application that takes a parameter num_points to calculate the value of Pi: 

from __future__ import annotations

import random
import sys

from my_modules.pi import is_point_in_the_unit_circle
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Check if the number of arguments is correct
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print("Usage: python script.py <num_points>")
        sys.exit(1)

    # Get the number of points from command-line arguments
    num_points = int(sys.argv[1])

    # Create a Spark session
    spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("Pi-Estimation").getOrCreate()

    # Generate random points within the unit square
    points = spark.sparkContext.parallelize(range(1, num_points + 1)).map(
        lambda _: (random.random(), random.random())
    )

    # Count points within the unit circle
    inside_circle = points.filter(is_point_in_the_unit_circle)

    # Estimate Pi
    pi_estimate = 4 * inside_circle.count() / num_points

    # Display the result
    print(f"Pi is approximately {pi_estimate}")

    # Stop the Spark session
    spark.stop()
and a Dockerfile to package the application with the spark image: 
ARG SPARK_IMAGE=apache/spark:3.5.9-scala2.12-java17-python3-ubuntu
FROM ${SPARK_IMAGE}

COPY my_modules /opt/spark/work-dir/my_modules
COPY job.py /opt/spark/work-dir/
ENV PYTHONPATH="${PYTHONPATH}:/opt/spark/work-dir"

Build the image from the repository root:

docker build -t pyspark-job examples/python

For a local cluster, load the image into one of the following cluster runtimes:

# Minikube
minikube image load pyspark-job
# Or kind
kind load docker-image pyspark-job

The supplied submission scripts use image_pull_policy="Never" (CLI: --image-pull-policy Never) for these preloaded images. For a remote cluster, replace the example registry below, push the tagged image, and update the script's image to that same name and its pull policy to IfNotPresent:

docker tag pyspark-job registry.example.com/team/pyspark-job:example
docker push registry.example.com/team/pyspark-job:example
Then, you can submit the job using the python client: 
from __future__ import annotations

import logging

from spark_on_k8s.client import ExecutorInstances, PodResources, SparkOnK8S

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    spark_client = SparkOnK8S()
    spark_client.submit_app(
        image="pyspark-job",
        app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
        app_arguments=["100000"],
        app_name="pyspark-job-example",
        namespace="spark",
        service_account="spark",
        app_waiter="log",
        # If you test this locally (minikube or kind) without pushing the image to a registry,
        # you need to set the image_pull_policy to Never.
        image_pull_policy="Never",
        ui_reverse_proxy=True,
        driver_resources=PodResources(cpu=1, memory=512, memory_overhead=128),
        executor_resources=PodResources(cpu=1, memory=512, memory_overhead=128),
        # Run with 5 executors
        executor_instances=ExecutorInstances(initial=5),
    )
or using the CLI: 
spark-on-k8s app submit \
  --image pyspark-job \
  --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py \
  --namespace spark \
  --name pyspark-job-example \
  --service-account spark \
  --image-pull-policy Never \
  --driver-cpu 1 \
  --driver-memory 512 \
  --driver-memory-overhead 128 \
  --executor-cpu 1 \
  --executor-memory 512 \
  --executor-memory-overhead 128 \
  --executor-initial-instances 5 \
  --ui-reverse-proxy \
  --logs \
  100000

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
This example is similar to the previous one, but it's implemented in java (with maven).

pom.xml: 

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>com.oss-tech.examples</groupId>
    <artifactId>java-job</artifactId>
    <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.source>11</maven.compiler.source>
        <maven.compiler.target>11</maven.compiler.target>
        <spark.version>3.5.9</spark.version>
        <scala.binary.version>2.12</scala.binary.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.apache.spark</groupId>
            <artifactId>spark-core_${scala.binary.version}</artifactId>
            <version>${spark.version}</version>
            <scope>provided</scope>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.apache.spark</groupId>
            <artifactId>spark-sql_${scala.binary.version}</artifactId>
            <version>${spark.version}</version>
            <scope>provided</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</project>
the job class (src/main/java/com/oss_tech/examples/TestJob.java): 
package com.oss_tech.examples;

import org.apache.spark.sql.SparkSession;
import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset;
import org.apache.spark.sql.Row;


public class TestJob {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    // Check if the correct number of arguments is provided
    if (args.length != 1) {
      System.err.println("Usage: PiEstimation <num_points>");
      System.exit(1);
    }

    // Initialize Spark session
    final SparkSession spark = SparkSession.builder()
        .appName("Spark Java example")
        .getOrCreate();

    // Get the number of points from command-line arguments
    final int numPoints = Integer.parseInt(args[0]);

    Dataset<Row> points = spark.range(1, numPoints + 1)
        .selectExpr("rand() as x", "rand() as y");

    // Count points within the unit circle
    long insideCircle = points.filter("x * x + y * y <= 1").count();

    // Estimate Pi
    double piEstimate = 4.0 * insideCircle / numPoints;

    // Display the result
    System.out.println("Pi is approximately " + piEstimate);
  }
}

Build the image from the repository root:

docker build -t java-spark-job examples/java

For a local cluster, load the image into one of the following cluster runtimes:

# Minikube
minikube image load java-spark-job
# Or kind
kind load docker-image java-spark-job

The supplied submission scripts use image_pull_policy="Never" (CLI: --image-pull-policy Never) for these preloaded images. For a remote cluster, replace the example registry below, push the tagged image, and update the script's image to that same name and its pull policy to IfNotPresent:

docker tag java-spark-job registry.example.com/team/java-spark-job:example
docker push registry.example.com/team/java-spark-job:example
Then, submit the job using the python client: 
from __future__ import annotations

import logging

from spark_on_k8s.client import ExecutorInstances, SparkOnK8S

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    spark_client = SparkOnK8S()
    spark_client.submit_app(
        image="java-spark-job",
        app_path="local:///java-job.jar",
        app_arguments=["100000"],
        app_name="spark-java-job-example",
        namespace="spark",
        service_account="spark",
        app_waiter="log",
        class_name="com.oss_tech.examples.TestJob",
        # If you test this locally (minikube or kind) without pushing the image to a registry,
        # you need to set the image_pull_policy to Never.
        image_pull_policy="Never",
        ui_reverse_proxy=True,
        # Run with dynamic allocation enabled, with minimum of 0 executors and maximum of 5 executors
        executor_instances=ExecutorInstances(min=0, max=5),
    )
or using the CLI: 
spark-on-k8s app submit \
  --image java-spark-job \
  --path local:///java-job.jar \
  --namespace spark \
  --name spark-java-job-example \
  --service-account spark \
  --image-pull-policy Never \
  --executor-min-instances 0 \
  --executor-max-instances 5 \
  --executor-initial-instances 5 \
  --ui-reverse-proxy \
  --logs \
  --class com.oss_tech.examples.TestJob \
  100000

docs.title: Driver configuration
docs.text:
This package manages Spark applications in Kubernetes by directly creating the driver pod and submitting the job in client mode. This approach bypasses some of Spark's built-in driver configuration mechanisms, causing certain settings to be ignored (e.g., spark.kubernetes.driver.podTemplateFile, spark.kubernetes.driver.label.[LabelName], ...).

To address this, the package provides internal implementations for some key driver configurations, ensuring greater control and flexibility when deploying Spark applications in Kubernetes.

docs.title: Driver service account
docs.text:
Instead of providing spark.kubernetes.authenticate.driver.serviceAccountName=<some-service-account>, you can use: 

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    service_account="<some-service-account>",
)

docs.title: Driver resources
docs.text:
Instead of providing spark.driver.memory, spark.driver.cores, spark.driver.memoryOverhead, you can use: 

from spark_on_k8s.client import PodResources

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    driver_resources=PodResources(cpu=1, memory=512, memory_overhead=128),
)

docs.title: Driver environment variables
docs.text:
The source version supports spark.kubernetes.driverEnv.NAME in spark_conf. The client copies these properties into the driver container's environment before creating the Pod. This also applies to the CLI and both Airflow operators, which use the same submission code. Install from source until a release includes this feature; see installation.

For example, a launcher that loads a YAML property mapping into spark_conf can use:

spark.kubernetes.driverEnv.DATABASE_NAME: dbname
spark.executorEnv.DATABASE_NAME: executor_dbname

The driver receives DATABASE_NAME=dbname; Spark independently sets DATABASE_NAME=executor_dbname on executors. A driver-only property does not add an executor environment variable. With job files, put these properties under spec.spark_conf; with the CLI, pass them through --conf.

Names must be nonempty printable ASCII without =. Values may be strings, booleans, integers or finite floats; booleans become true/false, and an empty string remains empty. Null, structured values and NUL characters are rejected before Kubernetes writes. SPARK_DRIVER_BIND_ADDRESS is managed from the Pod IP and cannot be supplied through spark.kubernetes.driverEnv.

An explicit driver property replaces a matching driver template environment entry, including its valueFrom reference. Explicit environment entries also take precedence over matching envFrom Secret/ConfigMap keys, including secret_values and driver_env_vars_from_secrets. Sidecar and init-container environments are unchanged. Kubernetes retains its normal $(NAME) expansion behavior for environment values.

Use these properties for non-secret settings: they remain ordinary Spark configuration in the driver arguments and may appear in Spark diagnostics. Offline plan output redacts their values in both environment entries and configuration arguments; raw ApplicationPlan.resources retains the actual values for inspection. For credentials, use Kubernetes Secret references in the driver template or the Secret options below.

Use secret_values to create an application-owned Kubernetes Secret. Its keys become environment variables in both the driver and executors; executor delivery uses Spark's spark.kubernetes.executor.secretKeyRef configuration. To import existing Secrets into the driver only, use driver_env_vars_from_secrets. 

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    secret_values={"EnvironmentVariableName": "some-value"},
)

docs.title: Driver volume mounts
docs.text:
Pass Kubernetes volume and mount objects to volumes and driver_volume_mounts. The Secret secret1, ConfigMap configmap1 and persistent volume claim pvc in this example must already exist in the application's namespace. Replace the host and NFS paths with resources available in your cluster:

from kubernetes import client as k8s

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    volumes=[
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume1",
            host_path=k8s.V1HostPathVolumeSource(path="/mnt/volume1"),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume2",
            empty_dir=k8s.V1EmptyDirVolumeSource(medium="Memory", size_limit="1Gi"),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume3",
            secret=k8s.V1SecretVolumeSource(
                secret_name="secret1", items=[k8s.V1KeyToPath(key="key1", path="path1")]
            ),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume4",
            config_map=k8s.V1ConfigMapVolumeSource(
                name="configmap1", items=[k8s.V1KeyToPath(key="key1", path="path1")]
            ),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume5",
            projected=k8s.V1ProjectedVolumeSource(
                sources=[
                    k8s.V1VolumeProjection(
                        secret=k8s.V1SecretProjection(
                            name="secret1",
                            items=[k8s.V1KeyToPath(key="key1", path="secret/key1")],
                        )
                    ),
                    k8s.V1VolumeProjection(
                        config_map=k8s.V1ConfigMapProjection(
                            name="configmap1",
                            items=[k8s.V1KeyToPath(key="key1", path="config/key1")],
                        )
                    ),
                ]
            ),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume6",
            nfs=k8s.V1NFSVolumeSource(server="nfs-server", path="/mnt/volume6", read_only=True),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume7",
            persistent_volume_claim=k8s.V1PersistentVolumeClaimVolumeSource(
                claim_name="pvc", read_only=True
            ),
        ),
    ],
    driver_volume_mounts=[
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume1", mount_path="/mnt/volume1"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume2", mount_path="/mnt/volume2", sub_path="sub-path"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume3", mount_path="/mnt/volume3"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume4", mount_path="/mnt/volume4"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume5", mount_path="/mnt/volume5"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume6", mount_path="/mnt/volume6"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume7", mount_path="/mnt/volume7", read_only=True),
    ],
)

docs.title: Driver node selector
docs.text:
Instead of providing spark.kubernetes.driver.node.selector.[labelKey]=<labelValue>, you can use: 

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    driver_node_selector={"labelKey": "labelValue"},
)

docs.title: Driver tolerations
docs.text:
Instead of configuring tolerations for the driver pod via a pod template file, you can use: 

from kubernetes import client as k8s

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    driver_tolerations=[
        k8s.V1Toleration(
            key="key1",
            operator="Equal",
            value="value1",
            effect="NoSchedule",
        ),
        k8s.V1Toleration(
            key="key2",
            operator="Exists",
            effect="NoExecute",
        ),
    ],
)

docs.title: Driver init containers
docs.text:
Instead of adding init containers to the driver pod via a pod template file, you can use: 

from kubernetes import client as k8s

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    driver_init_containers=[
        k8s.V1Container(
            name="init-container1",
            image="init-container1-image",
            command=["init-command1"],
            args=["init-arg1"],
        ),
        k8s.V1Container(
            name="init-container2",
            image="init-container2-image",
            command=["init-command2"],
            args=["init-arg2"],
        ),
    ],
)

docs.title: Driver host aliases
docs.text:
Instead of providing host aliases (entries added to pod's /etc/hosts file) for the driver pod via a pod template file, you can use: 

from kubernetes import client as k8s

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    driver_host_aliases=[
        k8s.V1HostAlias(
            hostnames=["foo.local", "bar.local"],
            ip="127.0.0.1",
        )
    ],
)

docs.title: Executor pod template
docs.text:
The package provides an enhanced way to configure executor pod templates compared to Spark's built-in spark.kubernetes.executor.podTemplateFile configuration.

Instead of manually creating ConfigMaps and managing volume mounts, you can use the executor_pod_template parameter that accepts either:

  • Template content as a string (YAML)
  • Path to a local template file

The package automatically:

  1. Creates a ConfigMap with the template content
  2. Mounts it to the driver pod (so the driver can validate the template)
  3. Configures Spark to use the template for executor pods
  4. Sets the driver pod as the ConfigMap owner, so Kubernetes cleans up the ConfigMap when that pod is deleted

These submissions use the locally preloaded pyspark-job image and the spark namespace/service account prepared earlier. For a registry image, change the image name and use IfNotPresent as described in the Python example above.

Using template content as string: 

executor_template_yaml = """
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: executor
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "4Gi"
        cpu: "2"
      limits:
        memory: "4Gi"
        cpu: "2"
    env:
    - name: CUSTOM_ENV_VAR
      value: "custom-value"
  nodeSelector:
    node-type: "compute-optimized"
  tolerations:
  - key: "spark-executor"
    operator: "Equal"
    value: "true"
    effect: "NoSchedule"
"""

spark_client.submit_app(
    image="pyspark-job",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    image_pull_policy="Never",
    executor_pod_template=executor_template_yaml,
)

Using local template file: 

# Save your template to a file, e.g., executor-template.yaml
spark_client.submit_app(
    image="pyspark-job",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    image_pull_policy="Never",
    executor_pod_template="./executor-template.yaml",
)

Via CLI: 

# Using template file
spark-on-k8s app submit --image pyspark-job --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py \
    --namespace spark --service-account spark --image-pull-policy Never \
    --executor-template ./executor-template.yaml

# You can also set it via environment variable
export SPARK_ON_K8S_EXECUTOR_TEMPLATE="./executor-template.yaml"
spark-on-k8s app submit --image pyspark-job --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py \
    --namespace spark --service-account spark --image-pull-policy Never

Note: executor_pod_template and executor_pod_template_path are mutually exclusive. Use executor_pod_template_path (or --executor-pod-template-path in the CLI) for a template path already available to the Spark driver. Do not configure both options, including through environment defaults.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This guide describes the current source. Follow the installation guide to choose between a published release and a source checkout. Example file paths below are relative to the repository root.

docs.title: Before submitting
docs.text:
Install the core package using the installation guide, and use that same Python environment for these commands. Choose either the Python or CLI example below; they submit the same kind of application.

Have these inputs ready:

  • Kubernetes credentials for the intended cluster and namespace. By default the client loads your kubeconfig's current context. Use SPARK_ON_K8S_CONFIG_FILE and SPARK_ON_K8S_CONTEXT to select them explicitly, or SPARK_ON_K8S_IN_CLUSTER=true when running with an in-cluster service account.
  • A namespace and driver service account with the permissions described below. The submitting client's credentials and the driver's service account are separate.
  • A Spark application image accessible to every node that may run a driver or executor, with the application file and its dependencies included. A local:/// application path names a file inside that image, not on your laptop.
  • Data and storage access for both driver and executors.

The submitter does not need Spark or Java installed locally. The application image must have compatible Spark, Java and application runtimes; use the Spark compatibility guide when choosing it. If you do not yet have an image, follow the Python or Java examples first.

docs.title: Set up the Kubernetes namespace
docs.text:
The client creates the Spark driver pod. The driver uses its Kubernetes service account to create and manage executor pods. The following examples use namespace spark and service account spark; the submitting client also needs permission to create the application resources in that namespace.

If your administrator has already provided that namespace and service account, skip the setup helper and use their names in the submission examples.

The optional setup helper creates the namespace if needed, a service account named spark, and a ClusterRoleBinding to the built-in edit ClusterRole. This grants that service account edit access across all namespaces. It is broader than a namespace-scoped Spark driver role. On a shared cluster, ask the cluster administrator to provision a suitably scoped service account instead.

Running the helper requires credentials that can list namespaces, service accounts and ClusterRoleBindings, create missing resources, and bind the edit role. Use it only when that cluster-wide grant is intended. See the Kubernetes RBAC documentation for the difference between RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings.

With Python:

from spark_on_k8s.utils.setup_namespace import SparkOnK8SNamespaceSetup

namespace_setup = SparkOnK8SNamespaceSetup()
namespace_setup.setup_namespace(namespace="spark")

With the CLI:

spark-on-k8s namespace setup -n spark

docs.title: Python client
docs.text:
Replace the image and application path with an image accessible to your cluster and an application file included in that image. The values below are placeholders:

from spark_on_k8s.client import SparkOnK8S

client = SparkOnK8S()
driver_pod_name = client.submit_app(
    image="registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/my-app.py",
    app_arguments=["arg1", "arg2"],
    app_name="my-app",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    app_waiter="log",
    image_pull_policy="IfNotPresent",
)

submit_app returns the driver pod name. The application ID is generated from the application name with a timestamp suffix and is available in the application list. For a private registry, configure image-pull credentials for the pods in your cluster.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
The CLI can submit applications and manage applications created by either the CLI or the Python client. Submit an application and stream its logs:

spark-on-k8s app submit \
  --image registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0 \
  --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/my-app.py \
  --namespace spark \
  --service-account spark \
  --name my-app \
  --image-pull-policy IfNotPresent \
  --logs --timeout 300 \
  param1 param2

The CLI example waits up to 300 seconds after submission and reports the final status. A timeout stops observation; it does not cancel the application. Confirm Succeeded and check the application's expected output before treating the run as successful. For JSON output, saved receipts and safe cancellation, follow Automation and run identities.

List applications to find their generated IDs:

spark-on-k8s apps list -n spark

To kill a running application, copy its actual ID from that output. The following ID is illustrative; my-app alone is the application name, not the generated ID:

APP_ID="my-app-20261107120000" # Replace with the ID from the application list
spark-on-k8s app kill -n spark --app-id "$APP_ID"

Check the help for further commands and options:

spark-on-k8s --help
spark-on-k8s app --help
spark-on-k8s apps --help

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
Install the api extra before starting the REST API and web UI. For local access:

spark-on-k8s api start \
    --host "127.0.0.1" \
    --port 8080 \
    --workers 4 \
    --log-level error \
    --limit-concurrency 100

List applications in the spark namespace:

curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/apps/list_apps/spark' \
  -H 'accept: application/json'

The console provides a searchable application list, status filters, namespace selection, application details, and confirmed stop/delete actions. It refreshes in the background without resetting your filters. The last successful fetch age and polling state help you recognize stale data. Counts and filters describe the applications loaded so far; use Load more when additional pages are available. Completed applications from the configured history server appear as archive entries without live-driver actions.

The driver-log view supports search, a configurable tail and frozen reading while new lines arrive. Its live buffer retains the most recent 10,000 lines. Download exports that buffered text; it is not a complete historical log archive. The excerpt preview lets you review and edit bounded text before copying or sharing it. Connection failures appear separately from log text, and a history-server outage leaves live applications available. JavaScript and CSS are packaged with the Python distribution; no CDN is needed.

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080/webserver/apps?namespace=spark and use Open Spark UI for an application submitted with ui_reverse_proxy=True in Python or --ui-reverse-proxy in the CLI. Its direct URL is http://127.0.0.1:8080/webserver/ui/spark/APP_ID; replace APP_ID with the actual application ID. The API process must be able to reach the driver's service. When placing the console behind a gateway, configure the browser and proxy boundaries, including the public WebSocket origin when needed.

Use --host 0.0.0.0 to listen on all network interfaces when deploying behind an appropriate service or proxy. Client URLs should use the server's reachable host or address, not the wildcard bind address 0.0.0.0.

docs.title: Deploy the API with Helm
docs.text:
The chart deploys the API, its Service and RBAC resources. Ingress and the optional Spark History Server are controlled by chart values. The chart's env list sets environment variables for the API and its Kubernetes client.

The published chart is released independently from this source checkout. Inspect the selected published chart's values before deploying it; unreleased chart fixes and defaults described below may not be present:

helm repo add spark-on-k8s https://hussein.awala.fr/spark-on-k8s-chart
helm repo update
helm show values spark-on-k8s/spark-on-k8s
helm install spark-on-k8s-release spark-on-k8s/spark-on-k8s \
  --values examples/helm/values.yaml

To use the chart from this checkout, render it for review first, then install that local chart. Set API_IMAGE_TAG to a compatible, tested image from the current source; the old 0.12.1 API does not implement the readiness endpoint:

helm template spark-on-k8s-release ./chart --values examples/helm/values.yaml \
  --set-string image.tag="${API_IMAGE_TAG:?Set a qualified API image tag}"
helm install spark-on-k8s-release ./chart --values examples/helm/values.yaml \
  --set-string image.tag="$API_IMAGE_TAG"

Choose one chart source for a release. The commands above use example values from this checkout; adapt them to your cluster and selected chart version. The source chart defaults to readOnly: true, namespaces: "*", a ClusterIP Service on port 8000, and disabled ingress. Set namespaces to a comma-separated string such as "spark" or "spark,analytics" to scope the chart-created Kubernetes permissions to those namespaces. Enable readOnly: false only if the API should be able to kill or delete applications. The separate web UI button settings control visibility, not Kubernetes authorization. The API has no built-in user authentication, and namespaces does not restrict the HTTP reverse proxy. Expose the API through access-controlled networking or an authenticating proxy.

The source chart supplies in-cluster Kubernetes configuration and the API bind address and port. It requires an explicit API image tag or digest; a published chart defaults to its appVersion tag. Using a local chart does not build or install the Python source into an image. Set image.repository and image.tag to the API image version you intend to deploy, or use image.digest to select verified image contents; the digest takes precedence over the tag. This is independent of the Spark application image passed to submit_app. Follow Chart deployment boundaries for scoped access, image selection and existing-release upgrades.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Set environment variables before starting the CLI/API process or importing the Python client: configuration values are read at module import time. The table below lists defaults in the current source, before chart or caller overrides. unset means no environment default (None); {}, [] and an empty string are distinct empty defaults. Use lowercase true or false for boolean settings.

Most client defaults also apply to the CLI. The six node-selector, label and annotation variables marked CLI are CLI defaults; Python callers should pass the corresponding driver_* or executor_* dictionaries to submit_app. If all three executor-count variables are unset, applications use two executors with dynamic allocation disabled. The two executor-template settings are mutually exclusive, including when supplied through environment variables.

JSON settings use JSON syntax, including double-quoted keys and strings. Packages and existing Secret names use comma-separated strings instead of JSON arrays:

export SPARK_ON_K8S_SPARK_CONF='{"spark.sql.shuffle.partitions": "8"}'
export SPARK_ON_K8S_APP_ARGUMENTS='["--input", "s3a://example/input"]'
export SPARK_ON_K8S_DRIVER_ENV_VARS_FROM_SECRET='spark-storage,spark-catalog'
export SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WEBSERVER_APPS_REFRESH_INTERVAL='10'

The named Secrets must exist in the application's namespace. Refresh values such as 10s are invalid because the setting is parsed as an integer.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Choose the package release before following examples. develop documents the current main branch, which can include features that are not yet on PyPI. For a published package, choose its matching documentation in the version selector. The Python package, API container and Helm chart have separate release versions.

docs.title: Published releases
docs.text:
Use a virtual environment with a Python version accepted by your selected release. Check its metadata on PyPI. For example, create and activate an environment on macOS/Linux using that Python interpreter:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Then choose one of these installations:

python -m pip install spark-on-k8s # Python client, CLI and helpers
python -m pip install "spark-on-k8s[api]" # Also install the REST API and web UI
python -m pip install "spark-on-k8s[airflow]" # Also install the Airflow integration
