These commands install from PyPI. They do not install this development branch or the repository's example files. Availability of other extras and features depends on the selected release. For an existing Airflow deployment, follow the Airflow guide in the matching docs.

docs.title: Current source
docs.text:
The current source requires Python 3.11 or newer. The core client and API are tested on Python 3.11–3.15. Airflow 3.4 is tested on Python 3.11–3.14; the legacy Airflow 2.11.2 CI profile uses Python 3.12. Use Airflow 3 for new deployments. The airflow, airflow-ui and connect extras require Python below 3.15. Installing one of those extras on Python 3.15 does not provide its integration dependencies.

The submitting machine does not need Spark or Java. The application container supplies its own Spark, Java and, for Python jobs, Python runtime. Check the Spark compatibility guide when selecting that image. The optional Spark Connect client uses a reachable server. Server creation and lifecycle use the base package; query readiness and notebook sessions need the compatible client extra.

Clone the repository to obtain the source and example files:

git clone https://github.com/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s.git
cd spark-on-k8s

With uv, choose one row below. Each command uses the committed lockfile and creates .venv in the checkout. Python 3.12 is used here so every listed optional integration has a supported interpreter.

Functionality Installation command Python client, CLI and job files uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups SQL submission uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --extra sql REST API and web console uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --extra api Spark Connect companion uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --extra connect Airflow integration uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --extra airflow Airflow 3.4+ integration with its native task tab uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --extra airflow-ui

Select multiple --extra options when needed, such as --extra api --extra sql. airflow-ui already includes the Airflow integration. A later uv sync selects a new profile and can remove unselected extras.

Run commands through that environment:

uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s --help

To use the bare spark-on-k8s and python commands in the other guides, activate .venv in your shell first. On macOS/Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

Alternatively, use pip in an activated virtual environment with a supported Python version. From the checkout, install . for core or select extras, for example:

python -m pip install ".[api,sql]"

This pip path resolves dependencies from the package metadata; it does not use uv.lock. Use the uv profile above when you need the checkout's locked environment.

docs.title: Check the environment and continue
docs.text:
Using the selected environment, confirm the installed package and CLI are visible:

python -c 'from importlib.metadata import version; print(version("spark-on-k8s"))'
spark-on-k8s --help

These checks do not contact Kubernetes.

Continue with Getting started to submit an existing application, or choose another route in Start here. Commands that reference examples/ run from the repository root. Contributor dependencies and the separate Airflow 2.11 environment are in Development and validation.

docs.title: Portable job files and offline plans
docs.text:
Use one versioned job definition from your laptop, CI, or an Airflow DAG. Job files need only the base package: no Airflow or API installation is required.

apiVersion: spark-on-k8s/v1
kind: SparkJob
metadata:
  name: daily-etl
spec:
  image: registry.example.com/team/spark-etl:1.0
  app_path: local:///opt/spark/jobs/etl.py
  namespace: spark
  service_account: spark
  executor_instances:
    initial: 2
  spark_conf:
    spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: 8
profiles:
  production:
    spec:
      namespace: production
      executor_instances:
        initial: 4
      spark_conf:
        spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: 32

spark-on-k8s job validate job.yaml --profile production
spark-on-k8s job plan job.yaml --profile production --output json
spark-on-k8s job submit job.yaml --profile production --output json

Validation and planning do not open a Kubernetes connection. Plans use the same resource builder as submission, with deterministic preview identifiers. They are illustrations, not reserved runs or manifests to apply with kubectl: owner references require the real driver pod UID and are attached during submission.

The display preview redacts Secret and ConfigMap contents, literal environment values, sensitive configuration keys, and application arguments. Review any custom metadata before sharing it; arbitrary user text can contain credentials in places no automatic redactor can identify. ApplicationPlan.resources is the raw in-memory representation and can contain secrets; use to_dict() for display.

docs.title: Profiles and settings
docs.text:
Profiles recursively merge objects and replace lists and scalar values. A selected profile is validated after merging. Unknown settings, duplicate YAML keys, aliases, invalid resource quantities, and incompatible executor allocation bounds are errors. Files are limited to 1 MiB. Resource memory and overhead are integer MiB; CPU values are positive whole cores. For dynamic allocation, an omitted initial count defaults to the minimum (or zero when only a maximum is given).

Settings under spec match the Python SDK names: image, app_path, namespace, service_account, class_name, packages, app_arguments, spark_conf, driver_resources, executor_resources, executor_instances, image_pull_policy, app_waiter, startup_timeout, ui_reverse_proxy, driver/executor node selectors, labels and annotations, driver_env_vars_from_secrets, and executor_pod_template or executor_pod_template_path, plus driver_pod_template and driver_container_name. Secrets are referenced by name; literal secret payloads are deliberately not a job-file field.

spec.spark_conf accepts spark.kubernetes.driverEnv.NAME for driver environment variables. See driver environment variables for conversion, precedence and Secret handling.

Job submission defaults to no_wait, namespace default, service account spark, two executors, and 1 CPU/1024 MiB memory/512 MiB overhead per pod. Job files do not inherit SPARK_ON_K8S_* submission defaults. Set spec.app_waiter: wait or log to wait, and optionally bound CLI waiting with --timeout SECONDS.

A driver or executor template may be a Pod mapping, inline YAML, or a .yaml/.yml filename. Local filenames resolve relative to the job file, not the current directory. executor_pod_template_path is a path visible to Spark, not a local file to upload. Application paths are also interpreted by Spark; local Python files are not bundled.

Choose cluster credentials explicitly when needed:

kubernetes:
  config_file: ./kubeconfig
  context: development

Or use kubernetes: {in_cluster: true} inside Kubernetes. The default uses the standard kubeconfig/current context. A custom kubeconfig filename resolves relative to the job file. Never commit kubeconfig credentials to source control.

docs.title: Python and Airflow
docs.text:
from spark_on_k8s.jobs import JobSpec

job = JobSpec.from_file("job.yaml", profile="production")
preview = job.plan().to_dict()
driver_pod = job.submit()

The same definition works with both supported Airflow versions:

from spark_on_k8s.airflow.operators import SparkOnK8SOperator
from spark_on_k8s.jobs import JobSpec

job = JobSpec.from_file("job.yaml", profile="production")
run = SparkOnK8SOperator(
    task_id="daily_etl",
    kubernetes_conn_id="spark_cluster",
    **job.to_operator_kwargs(),
)

For Airflow, use a job without a kubernetes section: the operator connection owns credentials. Set app_waiter to wait or log when downstream tasks depend on completion, and use the operator's existing deferrable option when appropriate.

docs.title: Validate every environment
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s job validate job.yaml --all-profiles --output json

This validates the base definition and every named profile, including relative pod-template files, without connecting to Kubernetes. The result lists each profile and returns a nonzero exit code if any fails. --profile and --all-profiles are mutually exclusive. Run this in your configuration CI; validating only a development profile does not validate production overrides.

docs.title: Review CPU and memory requests
docs.text:
Plans include a capacity summary derived from the generated driver requests and effective Spark configuration. It shows executor heap, explicit overhead, off-heap and PySpark allocations, executor counts and minimum/initial/maximum CPU and memory requests. Memory is reported in MiB and CPU in cores.

spark-on-k8s job plan job.yaml --profile production --output json \
  --max-cpu 12 --max-memory-mib 32768

Optional budgets fail when a requested maximum exceeds the limit or cannot be calculated. Executor templates, driver sidecars/init containers, invalid resource settings and unbounded dynamic allocation are called out instead of being silently estimated. The manifest remains the source for detailed review. Admission mutation, quota availability, scheduling placement, storage, GPUs and runtime-created resource profiles are outside this estimate. This is a request budget check, not a pricing estimate or an admission controller.

For promotion, select the cluster as well as the namespace:

profiles:
  production:
    kubernetes:
      context: production-cluster
    spec:
      namespace: analytics-production

The context name is a reference to externally managed credentials, not a secret payload. Namespace selection alone does not select a cluster. For Airflow, omit this Kubernetes section and use the reviewed Airflow connection instead.

docs.title: Jupyter notebooks on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Create a Spark Connect server from a local Jupyter notebook, run DataFrame and SQL queries on Kubernetes executors, reconnect after a planned kernel restart, and delete the recorded server. The notebook uses the existing server lifecycle SDK and independent Connect sessions; Jupyter runs on your machine.

Use the canonical example at examples/jupyter/spark_connect.ipynb with notebook_support.py beside it. You can also download the notebook bundle, notebook, or helper. These downloads are built from the same source as the selected documentation version. The bundle contains both required files; it does not include credentials or an environment.

docs.title: Prepare the cluster and client
docs.text:
Server provisioning is available in the current source and may not be in your installed PyPI release. Follow current-source installation and use a checkout matching the documentation version. Run the following commands from that checkout's root. The example does not create a cluster, namespace, service account, catalog or storage.

  • An administrator must prepare an existing namespace and Spark driver service account with permission to create and manage executors. See the namespace setup guidance.
  • Your Kubernetes identity needs access to create, read and delete the driver and Services, inspect executor resources and logs, and use pod exec and port-forward. The example's startup helper uses exec to wait for the Spark listener before opening a tunnel.
  • Install uv, Git and kubectl locally. Use Python 3.12 for this example; the optional Connect client supports Python 3.11–3.14. Local Spark and Java are not required by the thin pyspark-client.
  • Choose a Spark 4 image available to the cluster, for its architecture, containing the exact Connect server JAR. The commands below select Spark 4.3.0; the integration workflow also selects 4.0.5. Use the client/server pair selected below and consult the compatibility guidance.

The server exposes plaintext gRPC through a private ClusterIP Service. The example opens a notebook-owned tunnel bound only to 127.0.0.1; it does not expose a public endpoint. Use a trusted development cluster. Server authentication, TLS, data authorization and network policy remain administrator responsibilities. Kubernetes access does not provide isolation between clients of a shared server.

docs.title: Start an isolated Jupyter kernel
docs.text:
On macOS or Linux, create a separate environment using the repository's locked notebook dependencies and Connect extra. The optional JupyterLab frontend is installed into that same environment; it is not needed by the automated notebook runner.

This notebook uses these client/server pairs:

Spark server Thin client 4.3.0 (default) pyspark-client==4.3.0 4.0.5 pyspark-client==4.0.5

A newer client API can require a newer server even when a simple query works. In validation, client 4.3.0 passed readiness and range queries against server 4.0.5, but createDataFrame from local rows failed because that server lacked spark.sql.session.localRelationSizeLimit. This specific failure is why the notebook checks matching versions; it does not establish that every operation across different versions is incompatible.

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=.venv-notebook uv sync --python 3.12 --locked \
  --no-default-groups --group notebook --extra connect
uv pip install --python .venv-notebook/bin/python 'jupyterlab==4.6.6'
uv pip install --python .venv-notebook/bin/python --no-deps 'pyspark-client==4.3.0'
uv pip check --python .venv-notebook/bin/python
.venv-notebook/bin/python -c 'from importlib.metadata import version; client = version("pyspark-client"); assert client == "4.3.0", client; print("Connect client:", client)'

export IPYTHONDIR="$PWD/.venv-notebook/jupyter-state/ipython"
export JUPYTER_CONFIG_DIR="$PWD/.venv-notebook/jupyter-state/config"
export JUPYTER_DATA_DIR="$PWD/.venv-notebook/jupyter-state/data"
export JUPYTER_RUNTIME_DIR="$PWD/.venv-notebook/jupyter-state/runtime"
export JUPYTER_PATH="$PWD/.venv-notebook/share/jupyter"
mkdir -p "$IPYTHONDIR" "$JUPYTER_CONFIG_DIR" "$JUPYTER_DATA_DIR" "$JUPYTER_RUNTIME_DIR"
.venv-notebook/bin/python -m ipykernel install --prefix "$PWD/.venv-notebook" \
  --name spark-connect-notebook --display-name 'Spark Connect (Python 3.12)'

The kernel registration and notebook state stay in this environment instead of a user-wide kernel installation. Jupyter can still discover other configured kernels; select Spark Connect (Python 3.12) in the notebook. An existing Jupyter frontend can also use this kernel when configured with the same kernel search path. See the upstream kernel installation guide and Jupyter directory settings.

Do not install full pyspark alongside pyspark-client in this environment: both provide the pyspark Python import namespace. A later uv sync can restore the locked client version and remove the separately installed JupyterLab frontend. Both version choices explicitly select the client after the locked sync, matching the CI matrix even if a future lockfile selects a newer client. After resyncing, reapply the selected client version, reinstall the frontend, and check versions before launching a new kernel. Use the environment's executables directly so an implicit sync does not undo that choice. Normal source use is editable. CI installs the built wheel and checks the actual kernel interpreter and package location separately.

Set explicit cluster settings before launching Jupyter:

export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_KUBECONFIG=/absolute/path/to/kubeconfig
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_CONTEXT=your-kubernetes-context
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_NAMESPACE=your-prepared-namespace
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SERVICE_ACCOUNT=spark
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SPARK_VERSION=4.3.0
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_IMAGE=apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SERVER_JAR=local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_ARTIFACT_DIR="$PWD/downloads/jupyter-results"

To choose Spark 4.0.5 instead, override the thin client in this same isolated environment after the locked sync and before starting Jupyter:

uv pip install --python .venv-notebook/bin/python --no-deps 'pyspark-client==4.0.5'
uv pip check --python .venv-notebook/bin/python
.venv-notebook/bin/python -c 'from importlib.metadata import version; client = version("pyspark-client"); assert client == "4.0.5", client; print("Connect client:", client)'
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SPARK_VERSION=4.0.5
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_IMAGE=apache/spark:4.0.5-scala2.13-java17-python3-ubuntu
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SERVER_JAR=local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.0.5.jar

If changing an already running example, finish its server cleanup and stop its kernel first. Use a new artifact directory for the new run after confirming that cleanup; do not overwrite or discard the previous server receipt. Changing a Python package on disk does not replace a client already imported into a kernel.

Launch the notebook with the selected pair:

.venv-notebook/bin/jupyter lab examples/jupyter/spark_connect.ipynb

The helper reads these settings without changing your current Kubernetes context. When SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SERVER_JAR is unset, the helper derives local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-<version>.jar from the selected Spark version; override it for a different image layout. SPARK_NOTEBOOK_IMAGE_PULL_POLICY defaults to IfNotPresent; use Never only when the image is already loaded on the cluster's nodes. The notebook requests one small executor; adjust capacity for your workload rather than treating the example's resource settings as production sizing.

For the download, extract both files into a writable directory and open its spark_connect.ipynb using the same environment. Keep the helper beside the notebook. Keep the artifact directory until resource cleanup is confirmed; it contains the server receipt needed to reconnect or delete safely.

docs.title: Run, restart and reconnect
docs.text:
Run the numbered notebook sections in order:

  1. Sections 1–3: inspect the kernel and settings, create the server, save its receipt, and open the loopback tunnel. Query readiness performs a real action and verifies the remote application against the receipt. A Running pod alone is not query readiness.
  2. Section 4: run distributed DataFrame and SQL queries and display a bounded pandas result. The range sum is 49,995,000. The result table has books and games, each with quantity 3 and revenue 45.0. The notebook compares the reported executor hostnames with actual owned Kubernetes executor pods.
  3. Section 5: open an independent session, verify that temporary views and SQL settings do not leak into it, and recover from an intentionally invalid query.
  4. Section 6: close the client sessions and tunnel, save restart evidence and leave the server running. Use Kernel → Restart Kernel. Do not use Run All across this boundary.
  5. Section 7: resume in the new kernel. It restores the recorded server, establishes a new tunnel and session, and checks the same application and driver UID. The query returns the same sum. The previous session's temporary view is absent and must be recreated.
  6. Section 8: explicitly delete the server and wait for owned resources to disappear. The final notebook-result.json records status: passed, kernel_restart_verified: true, and owned_resources_remaining: [].

The creation cell refuses to create a second server when its receipt or pending creation guard exists. Do not delete these files to bypass the guard. Reconnect to the known server or complete its cleanup first. If receipt publication fails after creation, retain the full identity printed by the cell and the available server handle; resources can still exist.

The notebook's helper manages the tunnel separately from the SDK. Closing a session, tunnel or notebook does not delete the server. A readiness timeout also leaves the server running. Keep the receipt and inspect the existing resources before attempting another creation.

docs.title: Data and session boundaries
docs.text:
Where state lives What survives a notebook kernel restart Notebook variables and local Python objects Nothing in the old kernel; rerun imports and recreate variables Connect session temporary views and session settings A new session does not inherit them The Kubernetes driver and executor resources They continue until explicitly deleted or failed; the receipt identifies them Shared catalog and durable data Only what your separately configured catalog and storage preserve

Paths passed to Spark refer to the server/executor environment. Local notebook files, installed Python packages and credentials are not automatically copied to executor pods. Use shared storage reachable by both driver and executors, and install required connectors and worker dependencies in the appropriate image. Collect only bounded results with toPandas() or collect(): those results are transferred into the notebook process.

Spark Connect exposes DataFrame and SQL operations; classic SparkContext/RDD APIs are unavailable. The example proves these generated-data operations and notebook rendering, not every Python UDF, extension, storage connector or production catalog. See the upstream Spark Connect quickstart.

docs.title: Recover without notebook variables
docs.text:
The restart exercise deliberately closes sessions and the tunnel before restarting the kernel. It uses phase-one.json to prove that the kernel changed and the server did not. This is a planned restart test, not abrupt-crash recovery coverage.

If the kernel exits before that evidence file is written, server status and deletion still need only server-receipt.json and your cluster credentials. From the checkout, use the same environment and explicit cluster settings:

.venv-notebook/bin/spark-on-k8s connect server status \
  "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_ARTIFACT_DIR/server-receipt.json" \
  --kubeconfig "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_KUBECONFIG" --context "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_CONTEXT" --output json
.venv-notebook/bin/spark-on-k8s connect server delete \
  "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_ARTIFACT_DIR/server-receipt.json" \
  --kubeconfig "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_KUBECONFIG" --context "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_CONTEXT" --output json

Deletion requests cleanup; keep the receipt until the resources are observed absent. To continue work instead, use the receipt-only recovery instructions at the end of the notebook: restore ConnectServerHandle from the receipt's inner server mapping, open a new tunnel, verify readiness, and create a new session. That workflow does not require the planned-restart evidence file.

An abruptly terminated kernel can leave a tunnel process running. Inspect the example's tunnel process records and stop only the process you confirm belongs to that notebook; do not assume a recorded PID still identifies the same process. The SDK does not own tunnels. A failed driver also is not automatically replaced: inspect its recorded status and follow server recovery before creating a replacement with a new receipt.

Problem Next action Wrong kernel or import failure Select the registered kernel and check its printed interpreter and package versions Pending driver or listener timeout Inspect scheduling, image/JAR, service-account permissions and driver logs; retain the receipt Lost tunnel or readiness timeout Repair connectivity and retry readiness for the recorded server; do not create a duplicate Receipt or pending creation guard already exists Inspect the saved/partial identity and reconnect or finish cleanup; an uncertain response is not absence Same-name resource has a different UID Stop; inspect the ownership conflict instead of deleting by name

docs.title: Automated coverage
docs.text:
The Spark Connect Kubernetes workflow executes this exact notebook through a real IPython kernel, restarts that kernel at the marked boundary, and checks distributed execution, rendered table output, session separation, failure recovery and cleanup. It uses a built wheel on disposable kind clusters with matching client/server pairs 4.0.5/4.0.5 and 4.3.0/4.3.0. Its evidence includes the executed notebook and JSON results.

This automation covers notebook kernel execution and output. It does not click through JupyterLab's browser UI, test arbitrary extensions, or simulate an abrupt kernel/driver crash. Follow development validation for the runner and workflow; a failed or unexecuted matrix row is not passing runtime evidence.

docs.title: Know which identity is acting
docs.text:
The local client uses its selected kubeconfig/context; the API submits with its own Kubernetes identity. Driver and executor service accounts govern workload access to Kubernetes and external storage. An Airflow connection selects the submitter identity and is separate from the task UI's service credentials. A gateway authenticates callers; it does not make a shared API service account act as each caller. Use separate API deployments and namespaces for separate trust boundaries. Do not treat namespace filtering as tenant authorization.

The convenience namespace setup helper currently creates a cluster-scoped binding to Kubernetes' edit role. Administrators should provision a namespace-scoped RoleBinding for production deployments instead. Neither the chart nor this library is a cloud IAM administrator. Prefer workload identity and external Secret references to literal credentials in job files.

docs.title: Diagnose evidence before changing resources
docs.text:
Record the cluster context, namespace, application ID and driver UID with your incident. Distinguish application fetch time, diagnostic collection time and Kubernetes event time. Refresh before acting on an old view. Retained history can say Running after an application disappears; it is not current health. Incomplete reads, missing events and empty logs do not prove health or justify resubmission. Compare current and previous container termination reasons, scheduler events and driver/executor logs before increasing resources.

Use namespace-scoped commands, substituting only identifiers from the receipt:

kubectl --context CONTEXT -n NAMESPACE get pod DRIVER -o wide
kubectl --context CONTEXT -n NAMESPACE describe pod DRIVER
kubectl --context CONTEXT -n NAMESPACE logs DRIVER -c driver
kubectl --context CONTEXT -n NAMESPACE get events --field-selector involvedObject.uid=DRIVER_UID

Do not replay data writes, delete shared PVCs or repair streaming checkpoints based only on a pod failure. Keep images, job definitions and external data recovery procedures independently versioned.

docs.title: Back up optional history consistently
docs.text:
The SQLite history store is an operational index, not a job queue or durable source of submission truth. Restrict database and backup access because labels and operational metadata may be sensitive. A live database may use WAL files; copying only the .sqlite file while it is being written is not a safe backup. Use SQLite's online backup API (or stop all writers before a filesystem copy):

import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

source = Path("/var/lib/spark-on-k8s/history.sqlite").resolve()
backup = Path("/secure-backups/history.sqlite").resolve()
with sqlite3.connect(source.as_uri() + "?mode=ro", uri=True) as original:
    with sqlite3.connect(backup) as target:
        original.backup(target)
        assert target.execute("PRAGMA integrity_check").fetchone() == ("ok",)

Choose a new protected destination and test restoration with the exact package version in a disposable deployment. Confirm records and retention settings, then verify live Kubernetes state separately. There is no automatic migration, restore endpoint or claim of multi-writer/high-availability database support.

docs.title: Qualify an additional integration
docs.text:
Cloud identity, table formats, accelerators and new orchestrators need a named owner and a reproducible acceptance test before joining the supported matrix. Pin image and connector versions. Prove work runs in executors, verify actual output and a controlled failure, and exercise interruption/restart semantics. For storage, check namespace, mount ownership and persistence across driver replacement. For streaming/lakehouse jobs, distinguish pod recovery from checkpoint correctness, table commits, ordering and replay guarantees.

Prefer a small recipe using the existing SDK and receipts over another control plane. A migration assessor must report unsupported source fields; it must not silently translate unknown Spark Operator semantics. OpenLineage reports and Airflow run correlation are optional evidence, not proof that every data write committed. Deployment examples do not establish arbitrary multi-cloud or multi-tenant isolation guarantees.

docs.title: Authorization review matrix
docs.text:
Surface Authenticator / authorizer Effective cluster identity Actor attribution Local SDK/CLI Kubernetes credentials and RBAC Selected local or in-cluster identity Kubernetes audit configuration Standalone internal API External network/gateway controls API service account No built-in end-user principal Remote-enabled API and metrics Shared operator bearer and admission policy API service account Shared operator, not a tenant identity Airflow task tab Airflow session, task permissions, ownership checks Configured Spark API service identity Airflow task binding; separate API has its own controls Airflow DAG execution Airflow Kubernetes connection and cluster RBAC Worker/triggerer connection identity Task execution and Kubernetes audit configuration

Disabling Airflow tab writes only disables browser mutations; it does not prevent DAG tasks from submitting workloads. Gateway TLS alone does not establish all these boundaries. See browser and gateway checks for prefixes, static assets, HTTP, WebSockets and direct-backend isolation.

Recovery restores recorded observations through the backup point, then collection resumes from currently visible pods. It cannot reconstruct deleted pods or intermediate statuses during an outage. Readiness indicates current service health, not historical completeness. Diagnostics classify infrastructure evidence, not workload efficiency; neither a successful pod nor an empty finding list means a Spark job is tuned.

docs.title: Remote job submission
docs.text:
Remote submission lets an automation runner send an approved SparkJob to the API without loading a local kubeconfig. It is disabled by default. Enabling it also requires bearer authentication for the existing API, dashboard, static assets, proxies and WebSockets. Only the GET/HEAD liveness (/health) and readiness (/ready) probes remain public.

This is an operator API, not a multi-tenant authorization system. Its bearer token grants access to the existing read and management routes as well as admitted submissions. The submission policy restricts new jobs; it does not restrict an authenticated operator's existing list, logs, kill or delete permissions. Use a separate deployment and Kubernetes service account for each trust boundary.

docs.title: Configure the server
docs.text:
Install the api extra and configure the server's Kubernetes credentials as usual. Requests cannot supply a kubeconfig, context, client configuration or cluster endpoint. Create a random token, store it in a restricted file or Kubernetes Secret, and mount a policy file. Do not commit either deployment credentials or tokens to source control.

export SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_ENABLED=true
export SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_TOKEN_FILE=/run/secrets/submission-token
export SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_POLICY_FILE=/etc/spark-on-k8s/submission-policy.json
spark-on-k8s api start

The token must contain at least 32 printable ASCII characters without spaces; use a cryptographically random value such as one generated by secrets.token_urlsafe(32). Missing or malformed configuration prevents startup. Configuration is loaded once per worker; restart all workers when rotating the token or policy.

Terminate TLS at a trusted reverse proxy or gateway. Do not expose the backend's plain HTTP port outside that trusted boundary. For browser access, the gateway must authenticate the browser, protect write requests against CSRF, and inject Authorization: Bearer <server-token> on every HTTP and WebSocket request. Ordinary browser WebSockets cannot attach a custom authorization header themselves. The application does not accept query-string tokens or bearer cookies and does not place a token in the dashboard bootstrap. The gateway must remove client-supplied identity headers before injecting its own and keep the backend unreachable directly. In remote mode, the Spark UI and History Server proxies forward only content-negotiation, range and conditional-cache request headers. Bearer tokens, cookies, gateway identity headers and other credentials are not sent to application services. Log WebSockets use the server's Kubernetes client and do not forward browser authorization headers to pods. Standalone mode with remote submission disabled keeps its existing UI behavior.

The Airflow task UI also makes server-to-server console requests. It does not have a bearer-token configuration option. When the Spark API uses remote mode, set SPARK_ON_K8S_AIRFLOW_SERVICE_URL to an administrator-controlled gateway that authenticates the Airflow service and injects the operator credential, or use a separate internal API deployment with remote mode disabled and access restricted to trusted services. Browser gateway injection alone does not authenticate the Airflow backend's requests. Never put the operator token in browser configuration, task arguments or the service URL.

Apply least-privilege Kubernetes RBAC, Pod Security admission, namespace ResourceQuotas and network policy independently of this feature. Approved code and images must be trusted: this API does not sandbox the application's code or prevent that code from using its service account. Set ingress request/concurrency limits for the capacity of the server and cluster.

docs.title: Admission policy
docs.text:
This example uses an illustrative image digest; replace it with an image you own and have reviewed. Application code must already be present inside that image. Prefer immutable digests, because an exact mutable tag can point to different code later.

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "namespaces": {"analytics": ["spark-worker"]},
  "applications": [
    {
      "image": "registry.example.com/data/report@sha256:1111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111",
      "app_path": "local:///opt/jobs/report.py",
      "class_name": null,
      "arguments": [[], ["2026-11-07"]]
    }
  ],
  "limits": {
    "driver_cpu": 2,
    "driver_memory_mb": 2048,
    "executor_cpu": 2,
    "executor_memory_mb": 2048,
    "executors": 4
  },
  "spark_conf": {"spark.sql.shuffle.partitions": [8, 16]}
}

Namespaces and service accounts are exact pairs. Each application entry binds an exact image, local application path, optional Java class and approved argument lists. Omitting arguments permits only an empty list. Arguments are not arbitrary free-form input: an approved wrapper could otherwise use them to execute unapproved code.

Memory ceilings include memory overhead. Driver and executor limits apply per process; the executor count also bounds dynamic allocation, which must declare an explicit maximum. The ordinary portable job defaults still apply: one CPU, 1024 MB plus 512 MB overhead per process, and two executors. A policy below those defaults requires explicit smaller job values.

Remote requests reject pod templates, packages, secret imports, custom labels/annotations, node selectors, profiles, Kubernetes credentials and all other unsupported fields. Only these Spark tuning keys can appear in the administrator's explicit value allowlist:

  • spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
  • spark.default.parallelism
  • spark.sql.adaptive.enabled
  • spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled
  • spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold
  • spark.sql.broadcastTimeout
  • spark.sql.session.timeZone

Values must match the policy, including their JSON types. Kubernetes settings, classpaths, plugins, environment variables, remote files, resource overrides and arbitrary Spark keys cannot be enabled through that allowlist. The API validates the generated pod before writing resources, and uses only the server-configured client for both planning and submission.

docs.title: Submit from the CLI
docs.text:
The remote CLI needs only the core package and a YAML or JSON job file. It does not require the api extra, Airflow, or local Kubernetes credentials. The job's namespace, service account, image, path, class, arguments and resources must pass the server policy.

export SPARK_ON_K8S_API_URL=https://spark.example.com/team
export SPARK_ON_K8S_API_TOKEN_FILE=/run/secrets/spark-api-token
spark-on-k8s remote plan report.yaml
spark-on-k8s remote submit report.yaml --timeout 30

--api-url and --token-file override those variables. SPARK_ON_K8S_API_TOKEN is an alternative to a token file; prefer the file in shared environments. Tokens are never accepted as a command line argument. HTTPS certificate verification is mandatory. Plain HTTP is accepted only for loopback development. Redirects are refused so credentials cannot be forwarded to another location, and environment HTTP proxies are not used by this client.

Output defaults to one versioned JSON object on stdout. --output text prints a redacted plan or the submitted driver pod name. A successful submission returns HTTP 201 and this shape:

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "operation": "submit",
  "run": {
    "namespace": "analytics",
    "app_id": "report-0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef",
    "driver_pod": "report-0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef-driver"
  },
  "status": null,
  "error": null
}

The readable name prefix is shortened when necessary to leave room for the random run identity and Kubernetes driver suffix. Each request creates a distinct run; a plan does not reserve its preview identity. Submission returns after resource creation and does not wait for Spark to finish.

The CLI uses the automation exit codes: 0 for an accepted operation, 1 for a remote/API/transport failure, 2 for invalid local input, 4 for a missing/disabled remote route, 5 for a request timeout and 130 for interruption. Errors have schema_version, operation and error: {code, message}; command-line parsing errors still use Click's normal stderr output.

docs.title: HTTP contract and retry safety
docs.text:
Send the SparkJob document directly as JSON to POST /jobs/v1/plan or POST /jobs/v1/submit, with the bearer header. Both use the same admission rules. Plans return HTTP 200 with {schema_version: 1, operation: "plan", plan: {...}, error: null} and redact application arguments. Requests are limited to 1 MiB, and receiving the body has a 15-second deadline.

The remote CLI bounds responses to 4 MiB and applies a 30-second HTTP deadline by default, configurable up to 300 seconds. Stalled response headers or bodies are interrupted. Hostname resolution also depends on the operating system's resolver timeout. This timeout does not cancel a server operation or stop a Spark job.

Requests are never retried automatically. A timeout, disconnect or Kubernetes failure can occur after some or all resources were created. Inspect existing runs before retrying to avoid duplicates; partial resources may require operator cleanup. Idempotency-Key is explicitly rejected until a durable, shared idempotency implementation is available. In-memory deduplication would not be reliable across API workers or replicas.

Authentication failures return 401, admission denials 403, disabled routes 404, unsupported idempotency or invalid JSON 400, oversized bodies 413, unsupported content types 415, and invalid job schemas 422. Kubernetes conflicts return 409; other Kubernetes failures return 502. Errors contain a stable code and a human-readable message, never the Kubernetes response body.

Admission limits apply to each submitted job. They do not reserve shared capacity or account for concurrent accepted jobs. Enforce aggregate resources with Kubernetes ResourceQuota or your external admission system. A policy rejection, a quota rejection and a scheduler wait are different outcomes.

Namespace allowlists constrain the shared operator deployment. Every bearer holder retains management access within that deployment's exposed surface; the allowlist does not establish individual user or tenant identity. Use separate trust boundaries where independent authorization is required.

docs.title: Run history, readiness and metrics
docs.text:
The optional run recorder keeps a small operational history after Kubernetes driver pods disappear. It is separate from Spark History Server: it stores metadata, not Spark event logs, stages, executors' logs or replayable job definitions. The console's Recorded runs page lists recorded runs and filters them by namespace, last observed status and presence. It is read-only and does not offer kill, delete or replay controls for retained records.

History is disabled by default. When disabled, the application creates no database or background collector, and /runs/v1 and /webserver/runs return 404.

docs.title: Enable persistent metadata
docs.text:
Provision a writable directory on a local or block-backed persistent filesystem, then configure the API:

export SPARK_ON_K8S_RUN_HISTORY_ENABLED=true
export SPARK_ON_K8S_RUN_HISTORY_PATH=/var/lib/spark-on-k8s/runs.sqlite3
export SPARK_ON_K8S_RUN_HISTORY_NAMESPACES=analytics,batch
spark-on-k8s api start

The API service account needs permission to list pods in each configured namespace. Wildcards are not accepted; at most twenty namespaces can be configured. The recorder only requests pods labeled spark-role=driver and uses the server's existing Kubernetes credentials.

Use one API pod with persistent block storage. Multiple API worker processes in that pod can share one SQLite file: a database lease elects a collector, and a transaction checks its owner, generation and expiry before committing. A stale worker cannot overwrite a newer worker's snapshot. Worker shutdown cancels pending requests and releases the lease. After a crash, another worker can take over once the lease expires.

SQLite WAL requires reliable local filesystem locking. Do not use NFS, SMB or a database file copied independently to multiple replicas. This feature is intended for a small deployment, not distributed HA storage. Back up the database with SQLite's backup facility or during a clean shutdown; copying only the main file while WAL writes are active can omit committed records. Keep the directory private to the API process and back up the database according to your operational needs.

The store initializes schema version 1 transactionally and refuses an unknown future version. Configuration objects and credential source fields are not collected into the database. A missing/unwritable directory or an invalid configuration prevents recorder startup; the API does not silently fall back to ephemeral storage.

docs.title: What is recorded
docs.text:
Each run is keyed by its Kubernetes pod UID. Reusing a pod name or Spark application ID creates a separate record instead of overwriting the old run. Retained fields are:

  • UID, namespace, application ID/name and driver pod name;
  • driver image, Spark version and Kubernetes creation time;
  • first and last observation times, last observed pod phase, and the time the pod was first absent.

Raw pod specifications, annotations, arguments, environment variables, SQL and logs are not selected for storage. Names, image references and other retained identifiers are workload-controlled and can themselves contain sensitive data; the fixed field list is not a content redaction guarantee. The collector selects the designated driver container when a pod also has sidecars.

Disappearance is independent of status. A running pod that disappears remains recorded as last seen Running, with a disappearance time; disappearance does not imply failure or success. Previously observed Succeeded and Failed phases remain terminal. A pod with the same UID that reappears clears its disappearance marker. The recorder cannot recover pods created and deleted entirely between polls, statuses it never observed, or runs that predate its first successful scan.

A namespace snapshot commits only after every Kubernetes page succeeds. Authentication failures, expired/repeated cursors, page limits, malformed metadata, cancellation or timeouts do not mark unseen pods missing and do not publish partial results. Other namespaces can still be collected while time remains in the overall budget. The starting namespace rotates between cycles so one slow namespace cannot continually prevent later namespaces from being collected.

Observation intervals are not execution duration or utilization. Retained status counts include missing runs and are affected by polling and retention; they are not a success-rate denominator, a cost report, lineage completion or a compliance audit trail.

docs.title: Bounds and retention
docs.text:
All settings below are optional environment variables with the SPARK_ON_K8S_RUN_HISTORY_ prefix.

Suffix Default Meaning INTERVAL 30 Seconds between collection cycles, 5–3600. TIMEOUT 15 Overall Kubernetes collection budget in seconds, 1–300. REQUEST_TIMEOUT 5 Timeout per Kubernetes request in seconds, 1–30; the overall budget can interrupt it sooner. PAGE_SIZE 200 Pods requested per page, 1–500. MAX_PAGES 20 Maximum pages per namespace, 1–100. RETENTION_DAYS 30 Delete records not observed for this many days, 1–3650. MAX_ROWS 10000 Maximum retained records across namespaces, 1–1000000.

SQLite lock waits are bounded to two seconds per transaction. The lease includes the collection budget, poll interval and a safety margin. No new namespace scan starts after the collection budget expires. Retention is enforced after both successful collections and recorded failures. The oldest records by last observation are removed first when the row limit is exceeded; a small limit can discard useful history, including records for still-present pods. SQLite reuses freed pages, so deleting rows need not shrink the database file immediately. Logical retention is not physical erasure and does not expire independent backups. Define backup access and expiry separately.

Restart API workers to change these settings. Increasing page limits may increase memory use and cluster API traffic; use namespaces and quotas that match the deployment's scale.

docs.title: Read-only HTTP API
docs.text:
GET /runs/v1/config returns enabled namespaces and retention settings. GET /runs/v1 returns {schema_version: 1, items: [...], next_cursor: string | null}. Each item contains:

{
  "uid": "6fb31548-331f-4c94-bb51-b0af6b8cd263",
  "namespace": "analytics",
  "app_id": "daily-report",
  "name": "Daily report",
  "driver_pod": "daily-report-driver",
  "image": "registry.example.com/jobs/report:approved",
  "spark_version": "4.0.5",
  "status": "Succeeded",
  "created_at": "2026-11-07T12:00:00Z",
  "first_seen": "2026-11-07T12:00:15Z",
  "last_seen": "2026-11-07T12:04:15Z",
  "disappeared_at": "2026-11-07T12:04:45Z"
}

Creation time, image, Spark version and application ID can be null. Disappearance time is null for a present pod. Filters are namespace, status (Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, Unknown), presence (all, present, missing) and limit (1–200, default 50). Pass next_cursor back as cursor with the same filters. Ordering uses immutable first-observed time and UID, so updating an existing run does not move it between pages. Retention may remove rows between requests. Only currently configured namespaces are exposed, even if the database contains older records from another namespace.

In remote mode, history and metrics use the same operator bearer authorization as other API routes. The recorder does not introduce tenant-specific permissions.

docs.title: Health and Prometheus
docs.text:
/health remains a lightweight liveness probe. GET and HEAD /ready check actual pod-list access in the configured namespaces, with a five-second overall deadline. Without history, readiness checks the API's default namespace. With history, the recorder must also be initialized and have a recent successful snapshot for every configured namespace. The freshness window is twice the poll interval plus the collection timeout and ten seconds. Until the first successful scan, readiness is 503.

Both probes remain accessible without a bearer in remote mode. Readiness returns only {"status":"ready"} or {"status":"not_ready"} and does not expose namespace, database or credential errors. Failed readiness removes the pod from service traffic; liveness does not restart it merely because Kubernetes is temporarily unavailable.

Set SPARK_ON_K8S_METRICS_ENABLED=true to expose /metrics in Prometheus text format. It remains protected by the remote operator bearer when remote mode is enabled. Configure the scraper's authorization through its secret mechanism; do not place a token in a scrape URL. Metrics include:

  • spark_on_k8s_history_enabled;
  • spark_on_k8s_runs_recorded{namespace,status};
  • spark_on_k8s_collection_successes_total{namespace} and spark_on_k8s_collection_failures_total{namespace};
  • spark_on_k8s_collection_age_seconds{namespace} (-1 before any successful collection).

Labels contain only configured namespaces and five bounded status values. No application IDs, pod names, images or exception text appear in metric labels. Counters persist with the SQLite database.

docs.title: Helm configuration
docs.text:
The chart uses /health and /ready for liveness and readiness. To enable history, provision an existing ReadWriteOnce block-backed claim and allow the API's filesystem user to write it:

replicaCount: 1
autoscaling:
  enabled: false
namespaces: analytics,batch
runHistory:
  enabled: true
  namespaces: [analytics, batch]
  existingClaim: spark-run-metadata
  intervalSeconds: 30
  retentionDays: 30
  maxRows: 10000
metrics:
  enabled: true

The database is mounted at /var/lib/spark-on-k8s/runs.sqlite3. The chart requires a claim and explicit namespaces, rejects multiple replicas/autoscaling, and uses a Recreate rollout so two API pods do not compete for the claim. Existing environment overrides remain supported. Make sure history namespaces also have the pod-list permissions configured by namespaces or an externally managed service account. The separately configured sparkHistory chart section still refers to Spark History Server event logs.

docs.title: Spark compatibility
docs.text:
The client supports the Apache Spark 3.5 and Spark 4 container entrypoint. It creates a driver Pod and starts spark-submit in client mode inside that Pod; Spark creates the executor Pods. No Spark installation or Java runtime is needed on the machine running the Python client, CLI, or API.

The execution matrix covers the maintained 3.5 line, the first Spark 4 minor line, and the current Spark 4 release:

Spark Apache image tag Scala binary version Runtime Java Upstream Python minimum 3.5.9 apache/spark:3.5.9-scala2.12-java17-python3-ubuntu 2.12 17 3.8 4.0.5 apache/spark:4.0.5-scala2.13-java17-python3-ubuntu 2.13 17 3.9 4.3.0 apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu 2.13 21 3.11

The workflow pins these images by digest. These are selected test combinations, not the complete set of runtimes supported by Apache Spark. See the upstream requirements for 3.5.9, 4.0.5, and 4.3.0. Other Spark releases and custom images need their own validation. Spark Connect, custom schedulers, GPU workloads, and third-party connectors are outside this matrix. Connect has a separate server lifecycle matrix for Spark 4.0.5 and 4.3.0.

docs.title: Client and application runtimes
docs.text:
The spark-on-k8s Python package requires Python 3.11 or newer. That is separate from the Python and Java runtimes in the application image. The driver and its Python workers must use compatible Python versions and the PySpark version that matches the image's Spark distribution. The integration workflow runs the client on Python 3.11 and uses the Python runtime supplied by each Apache image.

When upgrading a Java or Scala application, match the Spark dependencies and Scala artifact suffix to the image. For example, Spark 4 uses spark-sql_2.13, whereas the selected Spark 3.5 image uses spark-sql_2.12. Use Maven's provided scope for Spark dependencies; the image supplies them at runtime. Match third-party connectors, such as Iceberg, to both the Spark minor version and Scala binary version supported by that connector.

Spark 4 also changes SQL behavior, including enabling ANSI mode by default. The client does not disable these checks. Validate application queries against the Spark SQL migration guide when upgrading.

docs.title: Build the examples with Spark 4
docs.text:
The example Dockerfiles default to Spark 3.5.9. From the repository root, build the Python example with Spark 4.3.0:

docker build -t pyspark-job \
  --build-arg SPARK_IMAGE=apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu \
  examples/python

For Java, change the compile-time dependencies as well as the runtime image:

docker build -t java-spark-job \
  --build-arg SPARK_IMAGE=apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu \
  --build-arg SPARK_VERSION=4.3.0 \
  --build-arg SCALA_BINARY_VERSION=2.13 \
  examples/java

The Java builder uses JDK 17, which can compile against both selected Spark 3 and Spark 4 distributions. The resulting application runs on the image's JDK. Load or push the resulting image and submit it using the example instructions. Do not replace the Apache image's entrypoint: the client relies on its driver command and Spark's executor command.

docs.title: Execution tests
docs.text:
The Spark runtime compatibility workflow creates an isolated kind cluster for each of the three versions. It installs the built client wheel, compiles a Java job against the image's exact Spark jars, and submits four small applications through SparkOnK8S:

  • Python worker computation and a DataFrame aggregation, including Secret-backed environment variables in both driver and executor.
  • Multiple SQL statements mounted in a managed ConfigMap, including a quoted semicolon and a checked aggregation.
  • A SQL error that must fail the driver and prevent the next statement from running.
  • A Java class entrypoint that performs and checks a distributed aggregation.

Successful jobs must create executor Pods owned by the driver. After every job, the test deletes the driver and checks that its Pods, Services, Secrets, and ConfigMaps are garbage collected. The workflow uploads logs, Pod status, events, and the execution result, including on failure. Each job uses one executor, a four-minute application deadline, and a 25-minute overall deadline. At most two matrix jobs run concurrently. The harness accepts only a kind context and creates and deletes its own uniquely named namespace.

Local Spark computation can also be checked without Docker. With JAVA_HOME pointing to JDK 21, run from a checkout:

REPOSITORY="$PWD"
RUNTIME_DIR="$(mktemp -d)"
uv venv --python 3.11 "$RUNTIME_DIR/runtime"
uv pip install --python "$RUNTIME_DIR/runtime/bin/python" 'pyspark==4.3.0'
cd "$RUNTIME_DIR"
"$RUNTIME_DIR/runtime/bin/python" -I "$REPOSITORY/tests/integration/spark/run_local.py" \
  --spark-version 4.3.0 --artifacts "$RUNTIME_DIR/results"

Repeat with PySpark 3.5.9 or 4.0.5 and JDK 17 for the other matrix rows. This executes Python, SQL, SQL failure, and Java workloads with local[2]; it does not validate Kubernetes submission, networking, RBAC, or resource cleanup. The Kubernetes workflow requires a working Docker daemon. Its run results are the evidence for cluster compatibility; local-mode results are separate evidence.

The JVM matrix compiles a Java class against each runtime image's Spark jars. This proves that selected workload, not compatibility of an existing Scala assembly or arbitrary third-party connector. Rebuild and test your actual application with the intended Java, Scala binary version, Spark jars and connector set before upgrading it.

docs.title: Spark Connect companion
docs.text:
Use an existing Spark Connect endpoint from notebooks or Python tools without creating a Kubernetes job for every interactive query. This companion creates independent client sessions. To create a server using the SDK or CLI, see Create a Spark Connect server on Kubernetes. For an end-to-end notebook that provisions a server, runs distributed queries and resumes after a kernel restart, follow Jupyter notebooks on Kubernetes.

Install the optional thin client in a Python 3.11–3.14 environment:

uv pip install 'spark-on-k8s[connect]'

The extra targets Spark 4 clients and keeps pandas below 3, as required for full upstream compatibility. pandas 2 has no Python 3.15 wheels, so this optional extra is limited to Python 3.11–3.14; the base SDK and CLI retain Python 3.15 support. For Spark 3.5 servers, install the base package and a matching pyspark[connect] version instead. Match client and server versions when possible. The base Spark-on-K8s CLI/SDK does not import PySpark or need Java. The Spark 4 thin client also needs no local JVM.

docs.title: Named connection profiles
docs.text:
Create connect.toml with endpoint addresses and references to credentials:

[profiles.production]
endpoint = "sc://spark.example.com:443"
tls = true
token_env = "SPARK_CONNECT_TOKEN"

[profiles.local]
endpoint = "sc://127.0.0.1:15002"
tls = false

Set the referenced token through your normal secret manager or shell environment. Profile files reject embedded credentials, connection-string parameters, duplicate keys, and unknown settings. TLS is enabled by default. Non-loopback plaintext connections require an explicit allow_insecure = true; use this only with a trusted network or an independently protected tunnel. TLS verifies server certificates using the upstream gRPC client. There is no disable-certificate-verification option.

spark-on-k8s connect check connect.toml --profile production --timeout 15 --output json

The check runs a small remote DataFrame action and reports the server's Spark version. It runs in a separate process with a total timeout, so an unavailable server cannot leave a stuck CLI. Exit codes are 0 for success, 1 for configuration/connection failure, 2 for CLI usage errors, and 5 for timeout. Error output omits gRPC details that could contain credentials. A timed-out session may remain until the server's session expiry policy cleans it up; the check never stops the shared server.

docs.title: Notebook and application sessions
docs.text:
from spark_on_k8s.connect import ConnectProfile

profile = ConnectProfile.from_file("connect.toml", profile="production")
with profile.session() as spark:
    assert spark.range(100).count() == 100
    spark.range(5).show()

Every context opens a separate Connect session and attempts to release it on exit, even when user code raises an exception. If both application code and release fail, the original application exception is preserved with a cleanup note. A release-only failure raises ConnectError; server-side session expiry remains the fallback. It does not reuse or stop another notebook session. After the generated-data example works, try your warehouse data (for example spark.read.parquet("s3a://warehouse/events/")) only after verifying the server has the required connector, storage permissions and data. Files and data paths are interpreted on the server. Cluster-wide state and static Spark configuration belong to the server; classic RDD/SparkContext APIs are not available through Connect. Authenticate and authorize the server with your existing gRPC gateway and identity system: profiles do not provide server-side isolation.

For local access to a private Kubernetes service, use your normal kubectl port-forward tunnel and the loopback profile. The helper never reads or changes your kubeconfig. connection_string() is available for advanced integration but can return credentials; do not log it. Profile representations contain only the environment-variable name.

See the upstream Spark Connect overview and client installation guide.

docs.title: Create a Spark Connect server on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Create a private Spark Connect server when you want notebooks or Python tools to share a long-running Spark driver. The server launches real Kubernetes executors using the existing submission machinery. The separate connection profiles guide covers client sessions and existing services. For the complete local notebook workflow, including an isolated kernel, planned restart and cleanup, use Jupyter notebooks on Kubernetes.

This feature creates one driver and its private Services in an existing namespace. It does not restart a failed driver or restore sessions after a driver replacement. Use a new server receipt when replacing a server. Server pools, admission queues, authentication gateways and the Helm chart are outside this lifecycle helper.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Prepare the namespace and driver service account using the existing namespace setup guide. The driver needs permission to create and manage its executors. The caller needs permission to create/read/delete driver pods and Services in that namespace.
  • Use a Spark 4 image containing the Connect server JAR. Specify its exact local:/// path; the helper does not download a guessed Spark/Scala artifact. Kubernetes integration tests cover the pinned Spark 4.0.5 and 4.3.0 images in .github/workflows/spark-connect.yml.
  • Creation, status and deletion use the base package and do not need local Java or PySpark. Install spark-on-k8s[connect] on Python 3.11–3.14 for query readiness checks and interactive sessions. A separately installed compatible Connect client can also be used; see the client installation boundary.

The generated Connect Service is ClusterIP, with no public load balancer or Ingress. It serves plaintext gRPC inside the cluster. Use it only within a trusted network; anyone able to reach it has access to the server's execution environment and data permissions. It is not a tenant-isolation boundary. An external TLS and authentication gateway remains an administrator responsibility. No credentials are stored in the server receipt.

docs.title: Create and connect from the CLI
docs.text:
Create a server and save its identity in a new file:

spark-on-k8s connect server create \
  --image apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu \
  --server-jar local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar \
  --namespace spark --service-account spark \
  --name notebook --executors 1 \
  --driver-memory 1024 --executor-memory 1024 \
  --receipt-file connect-server.json --output json

The result contains the private endpoint and a server handle. Creation means that Kubernetes accepted the resources; query_ready is initially false. The receipt is published atomically without replacing an existing file. Keep it for status, readiness and deletion: it records the driver and Service UIDs, not just their names.

Use --kubeconfig FILE --context NAME on each server command to select an explicit cluster. Otherwise, the project's usual Kubernetes connection settings apply. Server workload settings are taken from the server configuration, rather than inheriting unrelated batch-submission defaults from environment variables.

For a notebook on your machine, keep a separate terminal running a tunnel. Replace SERVICE_NAME with server.service_name from the receipt:

kubectl --namespace spark port-forward service/SERVICE_NAME 15002:15002

Use the same kubeconfig and context as the creation command. The tunnel is managed by you; closing it does not stop the server. Spark can take time to start after creation. If the tunnel exits with a connection-refused error during startup, inspect the driver logs and restart the tunnel once the gRPC listener has started. Create connect.toml:

[profiles.notebook]
endpoint = "sc://127.0.0.1:15002"
tls = false

Then verify this particular server and open a session:

spark-on-k8s connect server wait connect-server.json \
  --profile-file connect.toml --profile notebook --timeout 120 --output json

from spark_on_k8s.connect import ConnectProfile

profile = ConnectProfile.from_file("connect.toml", profile="notebook")
with profile.session() as spark:
    assert spark.range(100).groupBy().sum("id").first()[0] == 4950
    spark.sql("SELECT 'connected' AS status").show()

Readiness checks a real remote action and verifies the remote spark.app.id against the receipt. A successful query against a different server is rejected. Resource identities are checked again before reporting readiness. A Kubernetes Running phase alone does not establish query readiness.

Inside the cluster, use the returned private endpoint in a profile with tls = false and an explicit allow_insecure = true only for your trusted network. Files, connectors and data permissions belong to the server image and service account; your local notebook's filesystem is not automatically available there.

docs.title: Python SDK
docs.text:
from spark_on_k8s.client import ExecutorInstances, PodResources, SparkOnK8S
from spark_on_k8s.connect import ConnectProfile
from spark_on_k8s.connect_server import ConnectServerConfig

client = SparkOnK8S()
server = client.create_connect_server(
    ConnectServerConfig(
        image="apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu",
        server_jar="local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar",
        namespace="spark",
        service_account="spark",
        app_name="notebook",
        driver_resources=PodResources(cpu=1, memory=1024, memory_overhead=512),
        executor_resources=PodResources(cpu=1, memory=1024, memory_overhead=512),
        executor_instances=ExecutorInstances(initial=1),
        spark_conf={"spark.sql.shuffle.partitions": "4"},
    )
)
print(server.endpoint)
print(server.to_dict())  # Persist this identity before waiting.

# After establishing a tunnel to server.service_name:
profile = ConnectProfile(endpoint="sc://127.0.0.1:15002", tls=False)
client.wait_connect_server_ready(server, profile=profile, timeout=120)
with profile.session() as spark:
    assert spark.range(10).count() == 10

ConnectServerHandle.from_dict() restores a saved identity. For the CLI receipt, pass its inner server mapping: the file envelope is {"schema_version": 1, "server": {...}}. Resource options use the same PodResources and ExecutorInstances types as application submission. Additional Spark settings and packages are explicit; settings that would change the managed master, identity, driver networking, Connect port or resource contract are rejected before creating resources. The explicit exception spark.kubernetes.executor.request.cores accepts a positive Kubernetes CPU quantity no greater than the configured executor cores, so fractional scheduling requests are possible while executor cores remain managed by PodResources.

docs.title: Observe, stop and recover
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s connect server status connect-server.json --output json
spark-on-k8s connect server delete connect-server.json --output json

The SDK equivalents are connect_server_status(server) and delete_connect_server(server). Deletion requests shutdown of the recorded driver and cleanup of its owned Services/executors. It reports a deletion request, not instantaneous completion. Closing a client session or tunnel leaves the server running. Keep the receipt until Kubernetes has removed the resources.

Status reports observed resource presence and driver phase, including missing or terminating resources. Permission errors and unreachable Kubernetes APIs remain errors, not evidence that a server has disappeared. Destructive operations verify all recorded resource identities before issuing UID-conditional deletion requests; a stale receipt cannot delete a same-name replacement.

A readiness timeout exits with code 5 and leaves the server running. Inspect the driver logs or diagnostics, repair connectivity or configuration, and retry the check. Do not create another server simply because a readiness check timed out. Creation failures include their phase, available partial identity and cleanup outcome. If creation confirmed ownership of a driver and later setup fails, the helper attempts to remove only that owned driver. An uncertain create response is not permission to adopt or delete a resource by name. Failed or uncertain cleanup requires inspection of the reported resource identity before retrying.

Server CLI commands emit one versioned JSON document with --output json. Runtime failures retain the available server or partial run identity. Exit codes are 0 for an accepted operation, 1 for an operational error, 2 for CLI usage errors, 4 for a Kubernetes not-found error, 5 for a timeout and 130 for interruption. Interruption retains any confirmed partial identity and does not initiate extra cleanup. If it interrupts rollback or deletion already in progress, that request may have reached Kubernetes; inspect the reported cleanup outcome. Status can successfully report missing resources without treating that observation as a transport error.

For upstream configuration details, see the Spark Connect server configuration and Kubernetes client-mode requirements.

docs.title: SQL jobs without Airflow
docs.text:
The SQL client submits a local .sql file or inline statements using a PySpark image. Airflow is optional. Install the SQL extra from this source checkout:

uv sync --locked --extra sql

After a release containing this feature is published, install that release with python -m pip install 'spark-on-k8s[sql]'. The current source documentation may include features absent from the latest PyPI release.

Configure Kubernetes access, namespace spark, and service account spark as in Getting Started. Then submit a local file:

uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s sql submit \
  --image apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu \
  --namespace spark --service-account spark --name daily-summary \
  --file queries.sql --logs

Or submit inline SQL:

uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s sql submit \
  --image apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu \
  --namespace spark --service-account spark \
  --sql "SELECT 'quoted;semicolon' AS value; SELECT sum(id) FROM range(100);" \
  --executor-initial-instances 1 --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=2 --wait

Use exactly one of --file and --sql. --logs streams output and waits; --wait waits without streaming. Both return a nonzero CLI exit status when the application fails (exit code 3; timeouts use 5). Add --output json for the shared versioned submission receipt, or --timeout 300 to bound observation after submission. A timeout does not delete or stop the application. Without either waiter flag, submission returns before the job finishes. Use the regular app commands to inspect its status or logs.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
SparkOnK8S.submit_sql accepts the same submission options as submit_app, except app_path, app_arguments, and class_name, which the SQL runner manages:

from spark_on_k8s.client import ExecutorInstances, SparkOnK8S

client = SparkOnK8S()
pod_name = client.submit_sql(
    sql_file="queries.sql",  # Or sql="SELECT 1; SELECT 2;"
    image="apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    executor_instances=ExecutorInstances(initial=1),
    app_waiter="log",
)
print(client.app_manager.app_status(namespace="spark", pod_name=pod_name))

The return value is the driver Pod name, as with submit_app. Set dry_run=True to return an offline ApplicationPlan; its to_dict() preview redacts SQL contents and other ConfigMap data. Generated SQL mounts take precedence over matching mounts in a driver template. Explicit conflicting SDK mounts and nested driver-template mounts that could shadow the SQL files are rejected. SQL runs in a single Spark session and preserves temporary views between statements. The first failed statement stops execution and fails the application. Statements already completed are not rolled back: this is not a multi-statement transaction.

The client splits SQL before submission, preserving quoted semicolons and comments. It mounts the runner and a JSON statement list in a managed ConfigMap at /configmap; do not mount another ConfigMap there. The image needs PySpark, but does not need Airflow, spark-on-k8s, or sqlparse. Deleting the driver Pod removes the managed ConfigMap through Kubernetes ownership. Empty or comment-only SQL is rejected by the SDK and CLI.

SQL is plaintext in the ConfigMap and may appear in application logs. Use Kubernetes Secrets for credentials, and configure storage/catalog credentials through Spark settings or the SDK's secret options. Input and output data must be accessible to the driver and executors; a path on the submitting machine is not automatically uploaded. The SQL file itself is uploaded, subject to the Kubernetes ConfigMap size limit.

For scheduled and templated SQL, the Airflow operator uses the same runner. Jinja templating belongs to Airflow; the standalone SDK and CLI send SQL as provided. Review Spark compatibility before changing runtime images or connector versions.

docs.title: Locate a failed statement
docs.text:
The SQL runner records the local file basename (or <inline>), statement number and original starting line in a companion metadata file. It stops at the first failure and reports that location plus the Spark error condition when available. The runner no longer prints the complete query in its own progress or failure messages. Spark's own logs and displayed result rows can still contain data; apply your normal log-access and retention controls.

Earlier successful statements are not rolled back. For quality gates, run explicit Spark SQL assert_true(...) statements before writes where possible. A successful pod only establishes program completion, not business correctness.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Choose the outcome you need. The API and Airflow are optional: neither is required to submit a job from Python or the CLI. These routes describe the current source; first choose a published release or a source checkout.

If you already have a Spark application image and Kubernetes access, follow Installation, then Getting started. If you want to try the included data example before arranging cluster access, start with the local ETL route below. It runs Spark and Java inside Docker.

Your goal Prerequisites and owner Install/profile First observable success Next guide See a real ETL result locally Application author: source checkout, Docker and capacity for the documented 2 GiB container; no cluster Starter application image; no API/Airflow SPARK_STARTER_OK after Parquet output and replay checks ETL starter Submit an existing Python/JVM application Administrator supplies namespace, scoped service account and cluster access; author supplies a compatible image and reachable data Core package; sql extra for SQL Recorded driver identity, then terminal success and application output Getting started, job files, automation Explore an existing Spark Connect service Platform owner supplies endpoint, trust/credentials and permitted data; author uses a compatible client connect extra on its supported Python versions Bounded check succeeds against that endpoint Spark Connect Explore data from a Jupyter notebook Platform owner prepares namespace, driver permissions and trusted cluster access; author supplies a compatible image Locked notebook group plus connect; optional JupyterLab frontend Distributed query and rendered table, then reconnection to the same server after a planned kernel restart Jupyter guide and notebook Run dbt with temporary Spark compute Platform owner supplies Kubernetes access, shared warehouse and external Hive metastore Separate experimental dbt-spark-on-k8s package dbt completes and owned compute is observed absent Managed dbt Create an interactive Spark Connect server Platform owner prepares a namespace, driver permissions and trusted network access Base package for lifecycle; connect extra for queries Receipt identifies private resources; a real query verifies readiness Server setup Observe jobs in a browser Operator supplies API deployment, scoped Kubernetes access and access-controlled networking api extra or a selected API image/chart Console lists the expected namespace and opens a known run Local console, chart deployment Run a scheduled Airflow task Airflow owner supplies a supported installation, connection and worker/triggerer access; author supplies the job image airflow; airflow-ui for native Airflow 3 task tab Task runs an application and reaches its documented outcome Airflow

The Python version used to submit a job is separate from the runtimes inside its application image. Use the Spark compatibility guide for Spark, Java, Scala and application-Python choices; the base client needs no local JVM.

A local ETL check proves computation on its fixture, not cluster networking or storage permissions. For shared clusters, ask the administrator for namespace-scoped permissions before using the namespace setup helper: that helper's cluster-wide grant is intentionally broader. Driver and executor data access must both work.

docs.title: When the first attempt fails
docs.text:
What you observe Next inspection What it cannot establish No confirmed driver identity Check the submission error and doctor guidance; an ambiguous response may still have created resources Caller checks do not prove the driver's runtime access or that nothing was created Driver stays Pending Diagnose the known application using diagnostics; inspect scheduling, image and storage evidence An empty or incomplete report does not establish health Driver terminated or logs stopped Inspect its final status and diagnostic evidence; logs ending alone are not success A termination request does not prove a completed graceful drain Process succeeded but data is wrong Check application output assertions and input/replay assumptions; see starters Kubernetes success does not validate business results

Keep the generated run identity. Share only sanitized evidence with the relevant application or cluster owner. For project fit, compatibility and operating limits, read support boundaries.

docs.title: ETL and lakehouse starters
docs.text: The source checkout includes two small projects with data, application images, and portable job definitions. Each has real Spark execution checks; they are starting points for batch pipelines, not production storage or catalog installations. Run the following commands from the repository root.

docs.title: Order events to Parquet
docs.text:
examples/starters/etl/ reads JSON events with an explicit schema. It normalizes country codes, quarantines invalid amounts, countries, and timestamps, chooses the latest event per order, and writes three Parquet datasets:

Dataset Fixture result clean_orders 4 orders; o1 keeps its latest amount of 1,250 cents quarantine 4 invalid events with rejection reasons daily_revenue 1 January: France, 2 paid orders, 1,750 cents; 2 January: US, 1 paid order, 2,000 cents

Cancelled orders remain in the clean dataset but are excluded from revenue. Money uses integer cents and dates use UTC. Revenue stays on the original order date even when a newer event arrives on a later day; the fixture checks that case. Equal update timestamps use a deterministic record hash as a tie-break. Replace that rule with an authoritative event sequence if your source provides one. Replays overwrite only the three named datasets under the selected output prefix, so use a dedicated prefix for this job.
