This Parquet replacement is not an atomic multi-table transaction: do not run concurrent writers against the same output prefix.

Build and check the example without a Kubernetes cluster:

docker build -f examples/starters/etl/Dockerfile -t starter-etl:4.3.0 .
docker run --rm --network none --memory 2g --cpus 2 \
  -e SPARK_LOCAL_IP=127.0.0.1 \
  --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD/tests/integration/starters/check.py,target=/opt/spark/work-dir/check.py,readonly" \
  --entrypoint /opt/spark/bin/spark-submit starter-etl:4.3.0 \
  --master 'local[2]' --conf spark.ui.enabled=false --conf spark.driver.host=127.0.0.1 \
  /opt/spark/work-dir/check.py --case etl --project /opt/spark/work-dir/starters \
  --work-dir /tmp/starter-check --spark-version 4.3.0

The check runs the pipeline twice and reads the written Parquet data to assert those results. SPARK_STARTER_OK indicates success; output data in this disposable container is removed when it exits. The ETL check covers Spark 3.5.9, 4.0.5, and 4.3.0 in the runtime workflow. Use the matching SPARK_IMAGE build argument to test another supported image.

docs.title: Replayable Iceberg updates
docs.text:
examples/starters/lakehouse/ bootstraps two fixture orders and merges a batch containing a new order and two versions of an existing order. It deduplicates the incoming batch and updates a stored order only when the incoming timestamp is newer. Equal incoming timestamps use amount and country as deterministic tie-breaks; equal timestamps already stored in the table are not overwritten. The expected final rows are o1=1250, o2=500, and o3=2000 cents. Replaying the batch must leave those values and the row count unchanged.

This example uses Spark 4.0.5, Scala 2.13, and Iceberg 1.12.0. Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 publishes Spark 3.5, 4.0, and 4.1 runtime artifacts; it does not publish a Spark 4.3 runtime artifact. Do not use this jar with Spark 4.3. See the official Iceberg release artifacts.

Download the pinned jar, verify its published checksum, and build the image:

mkdir -p examples/starters/target
ICEBERG_JAR=examples/starters/target/iceberg-spark-runtime-4.0_2.13-1.12.0.jar
curl --fail --location --retry 3 \
  https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2/org/apache/iceberg/iceberg-spark-runtime-4.0_2.13/1.12.0/iceberg-spark-runtime-4.0_2.13-1.12.0.jar \
  -o "$ICEBERG_JAR"
printf '%s  %s\n' \
  '03b923f05fb7c9224dbf36a0a443726915a4b81fd9ff171e7c90395e992220294197918c3725076485f6e72bfdd4838d46599a37416ccdd77abc757330b02aff' \
  "$ICEBERG_JAR" | shasum -a 512 --check
docker build -f examples/starters/lakehouse/Dockerfile -t starter-lakehouse:4.0.5 .

The jar is bundled into the image; Spark does not need to download Maven packages at runtime. Check merges, replay safety, and reading the pre-merge snapshot:

docker run --rm --network none --memory 2g --cpus 2 \
  -e SPARK_LOCAL_IP=127.0.0.1 \
  --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD/tests/integration/starters/check.py,target=/opt/spark/work-dir/check.py,readonly" \
  --entrypoint /opt/spark/bin/spark-submit starter-lakehouse:4.0.5 \
  --master 'local[2]' --conf spark.ui.enabled=false --conf spark.driver.host=127.0.0.1 \
  /opt/spark/work-dir/check.py --case iceberg --project /opt/spark/work-dir/starters \
  --work-dir /tmp/starter-check --spark-version 4.0.5

The check verifies both the original snapshot and the current table contents. This is a single-writer demonstration. The bootstrap step is not a concurrent initialization protocol, and snapshot cleanup or retention policies are not configured. Set those policies before growing a real table indefinitely.

docs.title: Submit on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Configure namespace spark and service account spark as described in Getting Started. The job definitions mount the same PVC at /data in both driver and executor templates. This is required: a driver's local filesystem is not shared with executor Pods.

examples/starters/storage.yaml requests ReadWriteMany. Select an RWX-capable StorageClass for your cluster and ensure it grants write access to group 185. The templates set fsGroup: 185, but storage provisioners differ in how they apply ownership. For a single-node demo only, ReadWriteOnce can be used instead.

kubectl apply -f examples/starters/storage.yaml
kubectl -n spark get pvc spark-starter-data

Continue only when the claim is Bound. For a local kind cluster, preload the images; the job files use image_pull_policy: Never:

kind load docker-image starter-etl:4.3.0 starter-lakehouse:4.0.5
uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s job validate examples/starters/etl/job.yaml
uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s job plan examples/starters/etl/job.yaml --output json
uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s job submit examples/starters/etl/job.yaml --timeout 300
uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s job submit examples/starters/lakehouse/job.yaml --timeout 300

For another cluster, push the images to a registry it can access, then update the job files' image names and use IfNotPresent. Change the input and output paths for your own data. Data paths must be accessible to every Pod; the client does not upload local datasets. The same job files can be loaded with JobSpec and passed to an Airflow operator.

The lakehouse job uses a Hadoop catalog on the shared filesystem at file:///data/lakehouse. It requires a filesystem with appropriate atomic rename semantics. For object storage, configure a suitable catalog (for example REST) and storage connector instead of changing this local path to an S3 URI. Follow Iceberg catalog configuration and keep credentials in Kubernetes Secrets or workload identity.

Deleting a driver does not delete these output datasets or the PVC. The local checks and CI container checks validate Spark computation and data results; shared-storage provisioning and Kubernetes execution of these particular starter jobs still depend on the target cluster. The separate compatibility workflow also exercises actual Kubernetes submission and driver-owned resource cleanup.

docs.title: Adaptation contracts
docs.text:
The ETL example records the first matching rejection reason. When a row violates multiple rules, later reasons are not retained. Keep that precedence in mind when diagnosing upstream input; a production extension should use stable rule IDs and explicitly decide whether multiple reasons or raw records may be retained.

Latest-event deduplication is not point-in-time feature reconstruction. For example, a change received after a prediction timestamp must be excluded from that prediction's training features even when it is the latest update today. Replay determinism does not establish historical feature correctness.

For CDC adaptation, define an authoritative source sequence and deletion policy. Equal event timestamps, backfills and delete-then-reinsert events cannot be ordered safely by timestamp alone. This starter is a batch demonstration, not a database CDC connector contract.

Lakehouse before_snapshot/after_snapshot values are observed table state. They do not independently prove which writer committed a snapshot. Keep the single-writer restriction when interpreting the example as execution evidence.

To adapt an Iceberg example to Delta or Hudi, begin with a complete, reviewed connector configuration. Job profiles recursively merge maps: adding a Delta setting does not remove inherited Iceberg catalog keys. Inspect the effective plan before submission and qualify the chosen Spark/Scala/connector combination. A shared 1Gi demo PVC is a dataset/output mount, not a recommended Spark shuffle layout, production storage capacity baseline or data retention policy.

docs.title: Support and compatibility boundaries
docs.text: Spark-on-k8s submits and observes Spark applications using existing Kubernetes infrastructure. The Python client, CLI and optional integrations share that core. Use Start here to select the smallest installation for your task. This page describes source policy; consult the documentation matching your installed release for its available features and tested versions.

docs.title: What the project owns
docs.text:
Surface Supported contract Outside that contract Python Documented client methods, run handles, configuration types and documented helper imports Every importable private/internal object; thread-safe concurrent use of mutable client convenience properties CLI Documented commands/options and the versioned JSON/exit contracts identified in automation Parsing human progress/error prose or assuming every command returns JSON Job files and plans Documented schema/version and merge behavior in job files A GitOps reconciler, scheduler or proof of cluster admission Experimental dbt Separate managed-command adapter for pinned dbt Core/dbt-spark and Spark 4.3 SQL workloads Stable adapter API, Python models, dbt Fusion/Cloud/v2, automatic cluster/catalog deployment or hard-kill cleanup Airflow Documented operators, connection behavior, provider discovery and supported task UI integration A replacement scheduler, identity system or indefinite support for every Airflow generation API and UI Documented routes/configuration and shared console behavior User/tenant isolation from a shared operator token; see remote submission History Bounded metadata, readiness and recorder metrics as documented in run history Durable Spark logs, audit certification, HA database or submission transaction authority Examples The explicit assertions and runtime combinations attached to each example Certification of every cloud, connector, storage backend or application outcome

Kubernetes administrators own cluster access, admission, workload identities, capacity, storage and network boundaries. Application owners own dependencies, input/output correctness, replay safety and external side effects. A successful pod is not a data-quality certification. Spark Connect profiles support existing endpoints. The optional server lifecycle helper creates and deletes private single-driver servers; administrators retain responsibility for network access, authentication, capacity and replacement after failure.

docs.title: Compatibility and retirement
docs.text:
The installation matrix and Spark runtime matrix name the tested combinations. A dependency range is not evidence that every possible combination has been exercised. Optional integrations must identify their maintained workflow, test cost and review owner; accepting one does not promise every feature on every interface. Airflow 2.11 remains a legacy compatibility path; new deployments should follow the Airflow 3 guidance. Do not remove the legacy path silently.

For a change to a documented contract, state the previous behavior, replacement, affected releases and migration steps in the PR and release notes. Normally retain the old behavior or a usable compatibility path for at least one published release with a deprecation notice before removal. Security or correctness fixes may need an earlier break: explain the reason and operational consequence prominently. Additive JSON fields remain permitted where the existing schema tells consumers to tolerate them. An internal refactor does not need a deprecation notice unless it changes a documented import or observable contract.

Before retiring a Python/Airflow/Spark combination, record upstream support status, actual maintained test coverage, dependency constraints and the proposed replacement. Announce the decision in release notes; do not infer retirement from a failing CI job or silently delete the matrix row to make a build pass. There is no guaranteed support duration, response-time SLA or enterprise certification.

docs.title: Deprecation register
docs.text:
No public API removal or compatibility retirement is scheduled by this change. Airflow 2.11 remains supported by its existing legacy checks; its upstream status alone is not a removal announcement.

When a retirement is accepted, add a row with the affected contract, replacement, first notice release, earliest removal release and decision/migration link. Keep the entry through removal so users can trace the upgrade path. Until then, this register is intentionally empty rather than assigning speculative deadlines.

docs.title: Evaluate and report
docs.text:
For a deployment pilot, record the Python package version, chart version, API image digest and documentation revision separately. Charts and packages have independent release channels. A rendered chart is not evidence of a successful deployment; record what ran in your staging cluster, including one job, diagnostics and the recovery procedure if you enable persistent history. The release runbook defines how future release records should make these distinctions visible.

Use Discussions for usage questions, and issues for reproducible defects. Include sanitized versions and evidence, not credentials or private data. Security reports follow the private reporting policy. The deployment security boundary describes gateway, proxy and browser responsibilities.
